a: Go on your way
p: The Hebrew "lekh lekha" is used only twice in the Bible: here and when God asks for Isaac (22:2).
b: The command is lekh lekha, literally "go, for yourself" or "go, by yourself." The extra word is hard to carry into English. Rashi read it as "go for your own benefit and your own good." Others hear "go off on your own," since Abram must leave behind the three circles that gave an ancient person identity and safety: land, clan and father's house, each one closer than the last. The same two words come back only once, when God says "Go to the land of Moriah" and asks for Isaac (22:2). The story of Abraham is framed by two journeys into the unknown, and the second costs more than the first.

a: The LORD said to Abram
p: Genesis gives no reason for the choice. Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition all filled the gap.
b: Genesis never says why God chose Abram. Joshua 24:2 adds that Terah's family "served other gods" beyond the Euphrates. Later Jewish stories make Abram a young man who reasoned his way to the one God and broke the idols in his father's shop (Genesis Rabbah 38:13; compare Jubilees 12). The Qur'an tells a similar story: Abraham watches a star, the moon and the sun set and turns from them to their Maker (Qur'an 6:74–79), then smashes his people's idols and is thrown into a fire that God makes "cool and safe" (21:51–70). Christian readers stress the other side: the call comes first, by grace, and Abram's faith is a response (Acts 7:2–4; Hebrews 11:8). Stephen in Acts says God first appeared to Abram in Mesopotamia, before Haran, which is why the KJV translates "had said."

a: And be a blessing!
t: A blessing, or a command to be one?
p: The Hebrew verb here is a command, "be a blessing," not only a promise.
b: Most English versions turn the last line into a result: "so that you will be a blessing." The verb form is actually an imperative, "and be!" Hebrew can use an imperative after promises to express a purpose, so the usual translation is possible. But the command form gives Abram a task, not only a gift. The word "bless" (barak) and "blessing" (berakhah) occur five times in 12:2–3, answering the five times "curse" appears in Genesis 1–11 (3:14, 17; 4:11; 5:29; 9:25). Many readers see God's plan to undo the curse starting with one family.
orig: וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה (veheyeh berakhah), "and be a blessing"

a: whoever treats you with contempt
p: God's "curse" and the human "contempt" are different Hebrew words, and the blessers are plural.
b: English Bibles often write "curse those who curse you," but the Hebrew uses two verbs. The person who acts against Abram is meqallelkha, from qalal, "to be light": to belittle, despise or treat as nothing. God's answer is a'or, from arar, the strong word for putting someone under a curse. Notice too that "those who bless you" is plural and "whoever treats you with contempt" is singular. Many commentators, Jewish and Christian, take this as a hint that God expects the blessers to outnumber the despisers.
orig: מְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר (meqallelkha a'or), "the one belittling you I will curse"

a: All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you
p: The verb can mean the nations will be blessed through Abram, or will use his name when they bless.
b: The verb nivrekhu is in a form (Niphal) that can be passive, "will be blessed," or reflexive, "will bless themselves." The repeats of this promise use the Niphal again (18:18; 28:14) but twice a clearly reflexive form (22:18; 26:4). On the reflexive reading the nations will say "May God make you like Abraham," as Israel later blesses "God make you like Ephraim" (48:20); Rashi took it this way. The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, made it passive, and the New Testament follows it: Peter (Acts 3:25) and Paul, who calls this verse "told Abraham the good news ahead of time" (Galatians 3:8). The Plain English "find blessing" tries to leave room for both.

a: I will bless those who bless you
p: The promise is often quoted in debates about the modern State of Israel. Readers apply it in different ways.
b: Many evangelical Christians, especially Christian Zionists, read 12:3 as a lasting rule: nations and people who support the Jewish people, and today the State of Israel, will be blessed. Jewish readers have long applied it to the people of Israel, Abraham's children (compare Numbers 24:9, where Balaam repeats it). Other Christians, following Paul, say the promise is fulfilled in Christ, Abraham's offspring, so that all who believe, Jews and Gentiles, are "blessed along with Abraham" (Galatians 3:7–9, 29); on this view the verse is not about modern politics. Muslims honor Abraham (Ibrahim) as the friend of God and the father of both Isaac and Ishmael, and read the blessing as reaching all his believing children (Qur'an 2:124–129).

a: Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran
t: Did Abram leave before his father died?
p: By the Hebrew numbers, Terah lived 60 more years after Abram left. Stephen says Abram left after he died.
b: Terah was 70 when his sons began to be born (11:26) and died in Haran at 205 (11:32). If Abram was born when Terah was 70, Abram left Haran at 75 while his father still had 60 years to live. Stephen says Abram left "after his father died" (Acts 7:4). There are three answers. The Samaritan Pentateuch gives Terah 145 years at death, which fits Stephen (see the variant at 11:32). Some, from Augustine on, suggest Abram was a younger son born later, and is named first for his importance. Rashi says the Torah tells Terah's death first so that no one would say Abram left his old father, and adds that the wicked are called dead even while alive. The narrator wants us to feel that Abram's past is now closed.

a: the people they had gained in Haran
p: The Hebrew says "the souls they had made." The rabbis took it to mean converts.
b: Literally, "the nefesh (souls, persons) that they had made in Haran." In plain terms these are servants and slaves who had joined the household; "make" can mean "acquire," as with wealth (31:1). But the odd wording invited a famous Jewish reading: no one can make a soul, so these are people Abram and Sarai brought to faith in the one God, Abram teaching the men and Sarai the women (Genesis Rabbah 39:14; Rashi). From this grew the tradition of Abraham and Sarah as the first missionaries and the father and mother of converts.
orig: הַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ (hannefesh asher asu), "the souls they had made"

a: the great tree of Moreh
p: Shechem was an old holy place. "Moreh" means "teacher," and the tree may have been a place of oracles.
b: The elon was a large tree, an oak or terebinth (the KJV's "plain" follows an old misreading). "Moreh" comes from the verb "to teach," so this was probably the "teacher's tree," where people sought divine guidance; Judges 9:37 names a "Diviners' Tree" near Shechem. Shechem is Tell Balata, beside modern Nablus between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, a large walled city in the Middle Bronze Age (about 1900–1550 BC). It stays a key place in Israel's story: Jacob buries idols under the tree there (35:4), Joshua sets up a stone under it (Joshua 24:26), and Abimelech is crowned by it (Judges 9:6). Abram claims a Canaanite holy site for the LORD with an altar.

a: At that time the Canaanites were in the land
p: This aside sounds like it was written after the Canaanites were gone. Ibn Ezra noticed it 900 years ago.
b: The comment seems to look back from a time when Canaanites no longer held the land. The medieval Jewish scholar Abraham ibn Ezra (1100s) hinted at the problem: "it may be that the Canaanite took the land from someone else then; if not, there is a secret here, and the wise will keep silent." Spinoza later quoted him as evidence that Moses did not write every line of the Torah. Rashi read it differently: the Canaanites were then in the middle of conquering the land from the descendants of Shem. Traditional Christian and Jewish readers say Moses wrote it with Israel's coming conquest in view, or that a later editor added a few notes. Critical scholars see it as one of many signs of a writer living in the time of Israel's kings (compare 13:7; 36:31).

a: To your offspring I will give this land
p: God's first promise of the land is to Abram's "seed," a word Paul later reads as pointing to Christ.
b: The Hebrew zera', "seed," is a collective noun: one word for many descendants, like "offspring." God repeats the land promise to Abram again and again (13:15; 15:18; 17:8; 24:7). Stephen notes that Abraham himself never owned "even a foot" of it (Acts 7:5); his only plot is a grave (23:17–20). Paul argues that the promise was made "to your seed, not seeds," meaning one person, Christ (Galatians 3:16), while also knowing the word is collective (Romans 4:18). Jewish tradition reads the seed as Israel and the promise as Israel's lasting claim to the land. This verse is also the first time Genesis says the LORD "appeared" to anyone.

a: called on the name of the LORD
p: To "call on the name" is to worship and pray. Some Jewish readers took it as proclaiming God to others.
b: "Call on (or in) the name of the LORD" means to pray to God and worship him by his personal name. People first did so in the days of Enosh (4:26), and Abram does it at each altar (13:4; 21:33). The Targum renders it "he prayed in the name." Some Jewish readers, Ramban among them, take qara in its other sense, "proclaim": Abram announced the LORD's name to the people around him. The Talmud (Sotah 10a) puns on the word to say he "caused others to call" on God, inviting travelers to thank God after they ate at his table. Joel 2:32 and Paul (Romans 10:13) promise rescue to all who call on the name of the LORD.

a: with Bethel on the west and Ai on the east
p: Bethel was a major later shrine. Ai, "the Ruin," was probably a ruin in Abram's day.
b: Bethel ("house of God") gets its name from Jacob later (28:19), so the narrator uses the name his readers knew. It is usually placed at Beitin, about 11 miles north of Jerusalem, and later became the royal shrine of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 12:29). Ai means "the heap" or "the Ruin." If it is et-Tell, as most archaeologists think, the city there was destroyed about 2400 BC and stood empty until about 1200 BC, so in any date proposed for Abram it was already a ruin. That fits the name, though it creates a well-known problem for the conquest story in Joshua 7–8.

a: There was a famine in the land
t: Was going to Egypt a failure of faith?
p: God had just promised the land. Ramban said Abram sinned by leaving it and by endangering Sarai.
b: The narrator gives no verdict, and readers have divided. Ramban (1200s) wrote that Abraham "committed a great sin without meaning to" twice here: he left the promised land instead of trusting God to feed him there, and he put his righteous wife in danger to save himself; for this, Ramban said, his descendants were later enslaved in Egypt. Others count the famine among the ten trials of Abraham that the Mishnah mentions (Avot 5:3) and say he did what any shepherd had to do. Many Christian commentators read 12:10–20 as the first of several stories where Abram's faith falters right after a great promise, showing that the promise depends on God, not on Abram.

a: to live there as a foreigner
p: Abram goes to Egypt as a "ger," a resident foreigner without rights of his own.
b: The verb gur means to live somewhere as a ger, a resident foreigner. Abram never stops being one: in Canaan he calls himself "a foreigner living among you as a settler" when he speaks to the Hittites (23:4). His descendants will be foreigners in Egypt for generations (15:13), and the Law will tell Israel to love the foreigner "because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Exodus 22:21; Deuteronomy 10:19). Hebrews says the ancestors confessed that they were "foreigners and temporary residents on the earth" (Hebrews 11:13).

a: Please say you are my sister
t: The wife who is called a sister
p: Genesis tells this kind of story three times (12, 20, 26). Readers explain the repeats in different ways.
b: Abram passes Sarai off as his sister here and again in Gerar (20:1–18), and Isaac does the same with Rebekah (26:6–11). Traditional readers take these as separate events: Abraham says it was a standing plan (20:13), and Sarai really was his half-sister (20:12). Critical scholars see one old tale told in three versions, often assigned to different sources (J in chapters 12 and 26, E in chapter 20). Literary readers such as Robert Alter treat it as a "type scene," a pattern told with deliberate changes. E. A. Speiser once explained it from Hurrian contracts at Nuzi in which a wife could be adopted as a sister; later study of those texts (Samuel Greengus, 1975) showed they do not support that idea, and few hold it today.

a: Pharaoh
p: "Pharaoh" means "great house." Genesis never names the king, as Egyptians often did not.
b: The Egyptian per-aa, "great house," first meant the palace. From the 1400s BC it came to be used for the king himself, and only from about the 900s BC was it put before a king's name ("Pharaoh Neco," 2 Kings 23:29). Genesis and Exodus always say just "Pharaoh," with no name. Conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen argue this fits Egyptian use in the second millennium BC; others note that it may simply be the storyteller's choice to keep the focus on Abram. Since no king is named, the story cannot be dated from Egyptian records.

a: camels
p: Domestic camels show up in the southern Levant about 930 BC. Are Abraham's camels an anachronism?
b: Camels appear often in the ancestor stories (24:10; 30:43; 37:25). In 2013 Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef dated the earliest domestic camel bones at the copper mines of the Aravah Valley, south of the Dead Sea, to the last decades of the 900s BC, which fits camel caravans arriving in the region then. Many critical scholars, including Israel Finkelstein, take the camels as a sign that the stories were told or retold in the time of Israel's kings or later. Conservative scholars such as Kenneth Kitchen answer that camels were known, though rare, in the Near East much earlier, that Genesis presents them as luxury animals of the very rich, and that a few camels in the hands of one wealthy family would leave little trace. Martin Heide and others date the main domestication of the camel, in Arabia, to the late second millennium BC. The evidence for camels before 1000 BC is real but thin, and its meaning is debated.

a: struck Pharaoh and his household with great plagues
p: Famine, Egypt, plagues, and a Pharaoh who sends Abram away rich: the story previews Israel's Exodus.
b: The pattern is the same as the Exodus: famine sends the family to Egypt (47:4), Pharaoh takes what belongs to them, the LORD strikes Pharaoh with plagues (nega', the word used of the last plague in Exodus 11:1), and Pharaoh sends them away with wealth (Exodus 12:31–36). The rabbis said "what happened to the fathers is a sign for the children," and Genesis Rabbah 40:6 says God told Abram, "Go and pave the road for your children." Ramban built his reading of Genesis on that principle. Critical scholars agree the link is deliberate and see the story as shaped by the Exodus tradition.

a: What is this you have done to me?
t: A pagan king rebukes the prophet
p: Pharaoh asks God's own question: "What have you done?" The outsider sounds more righteous than Abram.
b: Pharaoh's words echo God's questions to Eve, "What is this you have done?" (3:13, literally), and to Cain (4:10). The same rebuke comes from Abimelech (20:9) and again to Isaac (26:10). Abram has no answer; he does not speak again in the chapter. The Genesis Apocryphon, an Aramaic retelling found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, softens the story: Abram has a warning dream and later heals Pharaoh by laying his hands on him and praying. Genesis itself lets the man of promise look worse than the foreign king.

a: very heavy with wealth
p: The word for "rich" is "heavy," the same word used for the famine that drove Abram to Egypt.
b: Hebrew kaved means "heavy." It describes the famine that "lay heavy" on the land (12:10), and now Abram himself, "heavy" with livestock, silver and gold. The same root gives kavod, "weight, honor, glory." The wordplay tells the story in two words: Abram went down to Egypt because of a heavy famine and came back heavy with Egypt's goods. Some readers hear irony: the wealth gained by Sarai's danger is what now splits the family (13:6).

a: The land could not carry the two of them living together
p: The words "brothers" and "live together" come back in Psalm 133: "how good when brothers live together."
b: The narrator uses the same Hebrew words twice: the land could not bear them "living together" (lashevet yachdav, 13:6), and Abram pleads "for we are brothers" (anashim achim, 13:8). Psalm 133:1 joins them: "Look how good it is, how lovely, / when brothers live together, all as one!" The same problem returns with Jacob and Esau, whose herds were too large for them to live together (36:7). In Genesis, wealth tests families as much as famine does.

a: The Canaanites and the Perizzites were living in the land at that time
p: The land was not empty. The Perizzites may be "villagers," people of the open country.
b: The comment reminds the reader that Abram and Lot are quarreling over grazing land that belongs to others (compare 12:6). "Canaanite" is a general name for the people of the land. "Perizzite" may come from perazi, "open-country villager" (Deuteronomy 3:5; 1 Samuel 6:18), so the phrase could mean "the city people and the village people." Both names appear in the standard lists of the land's nations (15:20; Exodus 3:8).

a: Isn't the whole land in front of you?
p: The older man, holder of the promise, lets the younger choose. Readers praise Abram's peacemaking.
b: As the elder and head of the family, Abram had the right to choose. He gives it away. Jewish tradition holds him up as a model of pursuing peace (compare Avot 1:12, "Be of the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace"). Christian preachers often contrast the two men: Lot chooses by sight, Abram by trust that God will give him what was promised (Hebrews 11:9–10). Some modern readers add that Abram may also be glad to be rid of a rival heir: Lot, his nephew, had been his likeliest successor.

a: like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt
p: Lot "saw" a land like Eden and like Egypt. Both comparisons hint that the choice will go badly.
b: Lot "raised his eyes and saw," the same way Eve "saw" that the tree was good (3:6). The plain looked like Eden, "the garden of the LORD," and like the Nile valley, watered without depending on rain. Both comparisons are warnings to a reader who knows the stories: people were driven out of Eden, and Egypt has just been a place of danger (12:10–20). The aside "before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah" tells us how this paradise will end (19:24–28). "Plain" translates kikkar, "circle," a word for the round valley of the lower Jordan.

a: moved his tent as far as Sodom
p: The KJV's "pitched his tent toward Sodom" is a famous sermon line, but the Hebrew says "as far as Sodom."
b: Generations of preachers have described Lot drifting slowly into sin: first he looks at the plain, then he "pitched his tent toward Sodom" (KJV), then he lives in it (14:12) and sits at its gate (19:1). The lesson may be sound, but the Hebrew 'ad means "as far as" or "up to." Lot moved his tents from place to place until he reached Sodom itself. Abram, by contrast, "settled in the land of Canaan," the land of the promise.
orig: וַיֶּאֱהַל עַד־סְדֹם (vayye'ehal 'ad-sedom), "and he tented as far as Sodom"

a: Now the men of Sodom were evil, great sinners against the LORD
t: A warning set beside Lot's choice
p: The narrator names Sodom's evil right after Lot chooses it, before saying what that evil was.
b: The sentence is placed like a shadow over Lot's choice. Genesis waits until chapters 18–19 to show what Sodom's sin was (see 18:20 and 19:5). The prophets later remember the city for pride, plenty, and neglect of the poor (Ezekiel 16:49–50) and for injustice (Isaiah 1:10). The Targums expand the verse: the men of Sodom were "wicked with their money and sinful with their bodies."

a: for all time
p: The Hebrew "ad olam" means "for a very long time," often "forever." It is central to modern debates.
b: 'Ad 'olam is often translated "forever." The word 'olam means a time so long that its end is out of sight; it can mean "for life" (a slave serves "for 'olam," Exodus 21:6) or truly forever (Psalm 90:2). The land promise is repeated as "to hold forever" (17:8). Jewish tradition and many Christians, especially dispensationalists, read it as God's lasting gift of the land to Abraham's physical descendants. Other Christian readers, following Hebrews 11:13–16 and Romans 4:13 (Abraham "heir of the world"), see the land promise widened to the whole renewed earth. The Law also makes keeping the land depend on Israel's faithfulness (Leviticus 26:32–33; Deuteronomy 28:63–64).

a: like the dust of the earth
p: God uses three pictures for Abram's descendants: dust, stars (15:5) and sand (22:17).
b: The promise of countless descendants comes in three images: the dust of the earth (here and 28:14), the stars of the sky (15:5; 22:17; 26:4), and the sand on the seashore (22:17; 32:12). Balaam, looking at Israel's camp, asks, "Who can count the dust of Jacob?" (Numbers 23:10). Solomon's reign is described as the promise kept: Judah and Israel were "many, like the sand beside the sea in number" (1 Kings 4:20). For a childless man of seventy-five with a barren wife, each image grows harder to believe.

a: walk through the land, its length and its width
p: Walking across a territory may have been a way to claim it.
b: God invites Abram to walk the land as its future owner. Some scholars see an ancient legal custom here: walking the boundaries of a property was a way of taking possession of it. God later tells Joshua, "Every place where the sole of your foot treads, I have given to you" (Joshua 1:3). Whether or not a formal custom stands behind the verse, the picture is of an owner looking over his property, though he still lives in tents.

a: the great trees of Mamre, which are at Hebron
p: Mamre, near Hebron, became Abraham's home base. Herod and Constantine both built there.
b: Mamre is named after Abram's Amorite ally (14:13). It is usually located at Ramat el-Khalil, about 2 miles north of Hebron, where Herod the Great built a stone enclosure around a sacred tree and well, and the emperor Constantine later built a church after finding pagan worship there (Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.51–53). Hebron, 19 miles south of Jerusalem, will hold Abraham's family tomb (23:19). The KJV's "plain of Mamre" follows the Aramaic Targum Onkelos, which rendered the word as "plain"; the Hebrew means large trees, probably oaks or terebinths.

a: Amraphel king of Shinar, Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of Goiim
p: The names look like real ancient names, but none of these kings is known from outside the Bible.
b: Shinar is Babylonia (11:2) and Elam lay in southwest Iran. The names fit the ancient world: Chedorlaomer looks like the Elamite Kudur-Lagamar, "servant of (the goddess) Lagamar"; Arioch resembles Arriwuk, a name found in the Mari letters (1700s BC); Tidal matches Tudhaliya, the name of several Hittite kings; Goiim means "nations." Nineteenth-century scholars identified Amraphel with Hammurabi of Babylon, an idea now abandoned. No inscription names any of the four as kings. Conservative scholars such as Kitchen note that coalitions of several kings were typical of the Old Babylonian age (about 2000–1600 BC), when a Mari letter says "no king is strong on his own." Many critical scholars think the chapter was composed late, with names chosen to sound ancient.

a: the Valley of Siddim, which is the Salt Sea
p: The narrator says the battlefield later became part of the Dead Sea.
b: "Which is the Salt Sea" seems to mean that the valley had since been covered by the Dead Sea, the Bible's "Salt Sea." The shallow southern basin of the Dead Sea, south of the Lisan peninsula, is often suggested; until the twentieth century it was under a few feet of water, and it is now mostly dry because of modern water use. The Dead Sea is the lowest place on land, about 1,400 feet below sea level, and its water is about ten times saltier than the ocean.

a: the Rephaim in Ashteroth-karnaim, the Zuzim in Ham, the Emim
t: The giant peoples of the east
p: These peoples were remembered as giants. The invaders march down the old King's Highway.
b: Deuteronomy calls the Emim and the Rephaim tall peoples "like the Anakim," and says the Ammonites called the Rephaim "Zamzummim," probably the Zuzim here (Deuteronomy 2:10–11, 20–21). Og of Bashan, who ruled at Ashtaroth, was "the last of the Rephaim" (Deuteronomy 3:11; Joshua 12:4). The invaders' route runs south from Bashan through Moab and Edom (Seir) to the gulf of Aqaba (El-paran), then back northwest to Kadesh and the Dead Sea. That is the line of the King's Highway, the ancient trade road east of the Jordan (Numbers 20:17).

a: they fell there
t: Did the kings fall or hide?
p: The king of Sodom "fell" into a tar pit, yet he is alive in 14:17. The verb may mean he threw himself in to hide.
b: The Hebrew says simply "they fell there." Since the king of Sodom meets Abram later (14:17), "fell" cannot mean "died." Some take it as an accident, others as a deliberate leap into the pits to hide. The rabbis told a story that the king of Sodom was stuck in the bitumen and rescued by a miracle, so that people would believe Abram's own rescue from the fire in Ur (Genesis Rabbah 42:7; Rashi). The Dead Sea was famous for its asphalt: the Greeks called it Lake Asphaltites, and Josephus describes lumps of it floating to the surface.

a: Abram the Hebrew
p: This is the first time anyone is called a Hebrew. The word may mean "descendant of Eber" or "one from across."
b: "Hebrew" ('ivri) appears here for the first time. Genesis links it to Abram's ancestor Eber (10:21; 11:14–16). It also sounds like 'avar, "to cross over," and the Septuagint translated it "the one who crossed over," that is, from beyond the Euphrates (compare Joshua 24:2–3). In the Bible foreigners usually use it of Israelites (39:14; Exodus 2:6; 1 Samuel 4:6). Texts from the 1300s BC, including the Amarna letters, mention the 'apiru or habiru, a class of uprooted people, raiders and hired soldiers across the Near East. Many scholars think the words are related, but the 'apiru were a social group, not one people, and the link to Abram is uncertain.

a: three hundred and eighteen of them
p: Jewish tradition found Eliezer's name in 318; an early Christian letter found the cross of Jesus.
b: A household of 318 fighting men shows that Abram was a powerful chief. Both Jewish and Christian readers found more in the number. The rabbis noticed that the letters of Eliezer, Abram's servant (15:2), add up to 318 (1+30+10+70+7+200), and said Abram went with Eliezer alone (Genesis Rabbah 43:2; Nedarim 32a). The Epistle of Barnabas (about AD 100) read 318 in Greek letters as TIH: T, shaped like the cross, and IH, the first letters of "Jesus" (Barnabas 9:7–8). Later tradition counted 318 bishops at the Council of Nicaea (AD 325). The narrator gives no hint of a code; the number simply fits a large household.

a: as far as Dan
t: A city not yet named Dan
p: The city of Dan got that name centuries after Abram, when the tribe of Dan captured it.
b: Dan, at the foot of Mount Hermon, was called Laish until the tribe of Dan conquered it in the time of the judges (Judges 18:29). Traditional readers who hold that Moses wrote Genesis say a later scribe updated the place name for readers, just as a modern book might say "the ancient site of Chicago." Some suggest a different, unknown Dan. Critical scholars see it as a plain sign that the story was written down after Israel's tribes had settled. Tel Dan has been excavated: its Middle Bronze Age mud-brick gate with three arches, from about 1750 BC, is one of the oldest standing arched gates in the world.

a: Melchizedek king of Salem
p: A priest-king who appears for three verses and vanishes. Jews, Christians and the Qumran scrolls all asked who he was.
b: His name means "my king is righteousness" or "king of righteousness," and Salem means "peace" (Hebrews 7:2). He has no parents, no ancestors and no death in the story, and readers have filled the silence. Psalm 110:4 promises a king "a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek." The Targums and the Talmud say he was Noah's son Shem, still alive (Nedarim 32b). One Dead Sea Scroll, 11QMelchizedek, makes him a heavenly figure who brings release at the end of days. Hebrews reads the silence as a picture of Christ: "with no father, no mother, no family line... made like the Son of God, he stays a priest for all time" (Hebrews 7:3). Most modern scholars see a Canaanite priest-king of the city that became Jerusalem.

a: Salem
p: Psalm 76 puts Salem in parallel with Zion. Most read it as Jerusalem; Samaritan tradition placed it near Shechem.
b: "His lair was in Salem, and his den in Zion" (Psalm 76:2) treats Salem as a short name for Jerusalem, and so do the Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran and Josephus (Antiquities 1.180). Jerusalem appears in Egyptian texts of the 1800s BC as Rushalimum, and later kings of the city had names like Adoni-zedek, "my lord is righteousness" (Joshua 10:1), much like Melchizedek. The King's Valley (14:17) is placed near Jerusalem in 2 Samuel 18:18. A Samaritan tradition instead put Salem near Shechem and Mount Gerizim, and some scholars have suggested other towns. Jerusalem is the common view.

a: bread and wine
p: Christians since the early church have seen a picture of the Lord's Supper. Rabbis saw temple offerings.
b: In plain terms, Melchizedek brings supplies to tired soldiers, the kind of welcome Gideon was refused at Succoth (Judges 8:4–6). Early Christian writers, such as Cyprian of Carthage (about AD 250), saw in the priest who offered bread and wine a picture of Christ and the Lord's Supper, and the Roman Catholic Mass recalls "the offering of your high priest Melchizedek" in its oldest eucharistic prayer. Hebrews, which says much about Melchizedek, does not mention the bread and wine. One rabbinic reading says Melchizedek taught Abram the laws of the priesthood, with the bread standing for the showbread and the wine for drink offerings (Genesis Rabbah 43:6).

a: God Most High
p: "El Elyon" was a known title in the region. Abram names the LORD as that God in 14:22.
b: El is the common word for "god," and also the name of the chief god of the Canaanites known from Ugarit. Elyon means "highest." An Aramaic treaty from Sefire in Syria (700s BC) names "El and Elyon" among its gods, so the title was known outside Israel. In the Bible "Most High" becomes a regular name for Israel's God, often in poetry (Numbers 24:16; Deuteronomy 32:8; Psalm 91:1). In 14:22 Abram calls on "the LORD, God Most High," identifying the God this priest serves with the LORD. Critical scholars see here how Israel took over and redefined an older title; traditional readers see a faithful worshiper of the one God outside Abram's family.
r: 14:22; Numbers 24:16; Deuteronomy 32:8; Psalm 7:17; Psalm 78:35; Daniel 4:17; Luke 1:32

a: maker of heaven and earth
p: The KJV says "possessor of heaven and earth." The verb can mean "create," "acquire" or "own."
b: The word qoneh comes from qanah, which usually means "buy, acquire" and so "own" (KJV "possessor"). But in some places it means "create" or "bring forth" (Deuteronomy 32:6; Proverbs 8:22), and a similar phrase, "El, creator of the earth," appears in a Phoenician inscription from Karatepe in Turkey (about 700 BC) and on a Hebrew jar fragment found in Jerusalem. So most translators now render it "Creator" or "Maker." Either way, the title claims that the God Most High is lord of the whole world, not a local god.

a: who has handed your enemies over to you
p: The verb "miggen" sounds like "magen," shield. In the next chapter God says, "I am your shield."
b: The rare verb miggen, "deliver, hand over," shares its letters with magen, "shield." In the next scene God tells Abram, "Do not be afraid, Abram. I am a shield for you" (15:1). The narrator links the two chapters with the sound: the God who handed the enemies over is the shield who will protect Abram.

a: And Abram gave him a tenth of everything
p: The Hebrew says only "he gave him a tenth." Hebrews reads it as Abraham honoring a greater priest.
b: The Hebrew says "and he gave him a tenth of everything," without naming the giver. Nearly all readers, including the Genesis Apocryphon, Josephus and Hebrews, take it that Abram gave a tenth of the spoils to Melchizedek; a few have suggested Melchizedek gave to Abram, which fits the grammar less well. This is the Bible's first tithe, before Jacob's vow (28:22) and the Law (Numbers 18:21–26). Hebrews argues that since Levi was still "in the body of his ancestor" Abraham, the Levitical priesthood itself paid tithes to Melchizedek, so his priesthood is greater, and so is Christ's (Hebrews 7:4–10).

a: I have raised my hand
p: Raising the hand to heaven was a way of swearing an oath.
b: The raised hand is the gesture of an oath, as when God "raises his hand" to swear (Exodus 6:8; Deuteronomy 32:40; Ezekiel 20:5). Abram has already sworn, or swears now, that he will take nothing from the king of Sodom. The contrast with Melchizedek is sharp: from the priest-king of Salem he accepts bread and wine and gives a tenth; from the king of Sodom he refuses even a shoelace.

a: so that you will never say, 'I made Abram rich.'
p: Abram will be made rich by God alone, not by the king of a wicked city.
b: Abram had earned a share of the spoil by the custom of war (compare 1 Samuel 30:22–25). He refuses, so that no one can say the king of Sodom made him rich. Jewish and Christian readers alike see this as a contrast with Egypt, where Abram did grow rich through a king (12:16). Ramban notes that he still lets his allies take their share: he will not impose his own vow on others.

a: the word of the LORD came to Abram in a vision
p: "The word of the LORD came to..." is how the prophets' books describe God speaking. This is its first use.
b: This formula opens the messages of the prophets: "The word of the LORD came to Jeremiah" (Jeremiah 1:4), "to Hosea" (Hosea 1:1). Its first use in the Bible is for Abram, whom God later calls "a prophet" (20:7). "Do not be afraid" is the usual first word of God or an angel to a frightened person (26:24; Judges 6:23; Luke 1:13, 30). After a battle and a sworn refusal of wealth (chapter 14), Abram has reason to fear revenge and poverty; God answers both fears.

a: Your reward will be very great
p: The KJV has God say "I am... thy exceeding great reward." The Hebrew more likely promises a reward.
b: The Hebrew reads "I am a shield for you; your reward very great." It can be taken as one sentence, "I am your shield, your very great reward," as in the KJV, which made God himself the reward, a favorite line of preachers. Most modern scholars take the second half as its own clause, "your reward will be very great," since Abram replies by asking what God will give him (15:2). Rashi links it to chapter 14: Abram refused the spoil of Sodom, so God promises him a reward of his own. "Shield" (magen) echoes the verb "handed over" (miggen) in 14:20.
orig: שְׂכָרְךָ הַרְבֵּה מְאֹד (sekharekha harbeh me'od), "your reward much very"

a: Lord GOD
p: Abram is the first person in the Bible to call God "Adonai YHWH." English Bibles print it "Lord GOD."
b: Abram addresses God as Adonai YHWH, "my Lord, YHWH," the first time this pair appears. Because Jewish readers say Adonai ("Lord") in place of the divine name, saying "Adonai Adonai" would sound strange, so the scribes gave YHWH here the vowels of Elohim ("God"), and it is read "Adonai Elohim." English Bibles follow by printing "Lord GOD," with GOD in capitals. Throughout the Plain English, "the LORD" in capitals stands for the name YHWH, "Lord" for Adonai, and "God" for Elohim or El. The title is one of humble address, often used in prayers of pleading (Deuteronomy 3:24; Judges 6:22).

a: the one who will own my household is Eliezer of Damascus
p: The Hebrew is a pun that nobody fully understands. The meaning is clear: a servant will inherit.
b: Literally, "the son of meshek of my house, he is Damascus Eliezer." Meshek appears nowhere else and seems chosen to sound like Dammeseq, Damascus. Most take it as "the one who will possess my house." Verse 3 restates it plainly: "a son of my house," a servant born in the household, "will be my heir." In the ancient Near East a childless man could adopt a servant or another man as his heir; texts from Nuzi (1400s BC) were once held up as close parallels, though the match is less exact than scholars like Cyrus Gordon first thought. Jewish tradition identified Eliezer with the unnamed servant who finds Rebekah in chapter 24.
orig: וּבֶן־מֶשֶׁק בֵּיתִי הוּא דַּמֶּשֶׂק אֱלִיעֶזֶר (uven-meshek beti hu dammeseq eli'ezer)

a: number the stars, if you can number them
p: The stars become the Bible's picture of the promise. The rabbis said God lifted Abram above the stars.
b: A clear night sky away from cities shows a few thousand stars to the eye, but for the ancients the stars were the very picture of the countless (Jeremiah 33:22). Moses tells Israel, "today you are like the stars of the sky in number" (Deuteronomy 1:10), and Hebrews and Romans quote the promise (Hebrews 11:12; Romans 4:18). The rabbis noticed that God "brought him outside" and said Abram had read in the stars that he would have no son; God lifted him above the stars' power: "Israel is not under the stars" (Shabbat 156a; Genesis Rabbah 44:12; Rashi).

a: Abram put his trust in the LORD
p: The verb is from the root of "amen": Abram leaned his weight on God's word.
b: He'emin, "he believed, trusted," comes from the root 'aman, "to be firm, reliable," the root of "amen" and of emunah, "faithfulness." To believe in this sense is to treat someone as solid and rest on what they say. It is not only agreeing that God exists; it is trusting a promise that has no visible support. The verb form suggests a lasting stance, not one moment. Isaiah plays on the same root: "If you do not hold firm in trust, you will not be held firm" (Isaiah 7:9).

a: he reckoned it to him as righteousness
p: The Hebrew says only "he reckoned it to him." Most read God as the subject; some read Abram. The Greek made it passive.
b: The verb vayyachsheveha, "and he reckoned it," has no named subject. "Reckon" (chashav) is an accounting word, used for crediting sacrifices (Leviticus 7:18). On the usual reading, God credits Abram's trust to him as righteousness. Ramban and some modern scholars read Abram as the subject: Abram counted God's promise as God's righteousness, his faithful kindness. The Septuagint makes the verb passive, "and it was reckoned to him as righteousness," and that is the form Paul and James quote (Romans 4:3; Galatians 3:6; James 2:23), so the subject question never arises in the New Testament. Psalm 106:31 uses the same words of Phinehas's zeal, a deed rather than a belief. The Plain English keeps "he" so as not to settle the question in the text.
r: Romans 4:3–12; Romans 4:20–24; Galatians 3:6–9; James 2:21–23; Psalm 106:31; Hebrews 11:8–12

a: Ur of the Chaldeans
p: Most place Ur in southern Iraq. Another tradition, held by many Muslims and Jews, places it at Urfa in Turkey.
b: The famous Ur is Tell el-Muqayyar in southern Iraq, excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s and 1930s: a great Sumerian city with royal tombs and a ziggurat to the moon god. Haran, where Terah's family settled, was also a center of moon worship. Some scholars, among them Cyrus Gordon, argued for a northern Ur near Haran, and a strong Jewish, Christian and Muslim tradition puts Abraham's birthplace at Urfa (Şanlıurfa) in southeast Turkey, whose "Pools of Abraham" honor the story of his rescue from Nimrod's fire. "Of the Chaldeans" uses the name of a people known in Babylonia only from about 900 BC, which many take as the narrator's later label. The Septuagint says "the land of the Chaldeans" (see the variant).

a: cut them in two down the middle
p: Ancient treaties were sealed by cutting animals in two. Whoever passed between them invited the same fate.
b: Jeremiah describes the same rite: leaders who "cut the calf in two and passed between its parts" and then broke their oath would be given to their enemies (Jeremiah 34:18–20). The meaning is a self-curse: "May I be cut in two like these animals if I break my word." An Aramaic treaty from Sefire (700s BC) says "as this calf is cut in two, so may Mati'el be cut in two." Letters from Mari (1700s BC) speak of making a treaty by "killing a donkey foal." The animals here are the same kinds later used for Israel's sacrifices.

a: Birds of prey came down on the carcasses
p: Abram guards the sacrifice through the day. Jewish readers saw the birds as a sign of enemy nations.
b: The plain picture is Abram waiting, perhaps all day, keeping scavengers off the pieces until God acts. Rashi and the Midrash read the unclean birds as a sign of the nations that would try to destroy Abram's descendants, and Abram's driving them off as a sign that the covenant would protect them. The next verses do speak of a foreign nation oppressing his offspring (15:13).

a: a deep sleep fell on Abram
p: The same word is used for Adam's sleep when God made Eve.
b: Tardemah is a heavy, God-sent sleep. God put Adam into one before forming the woman (2:21), and sent one on Saul's camp (1 Samuel 26:12). Here it opens Abram to a vision. The Septuagint translated it ekstasis, "trance." The "terror of great darkness" was read by the Midrash as a vision of the four empires that would rule Israel: Babylon, Media, Greece and Rome (Genesis Rabbah 44:17; compare Daniel 7).

a: they will be oppressed for four hundred years
p: Genesis says 400 years; Exodus says Israel lived 430 years in Egypt; Paul counts 430 from the promise.
b: God foretells slavery in Egypt "four hundred years," a round number (Acts 7:6). Exodus 12:40 says Israel lived in Egypt 430 years, but the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch there read "in Egypt and in Canaan," counting from Abraham. Paul also counts 430 years from the promise to the Law (Galatians 3:17), and Josephus gives both figures. Rashi counted the 400 from Isaac's birth. The "fourth generation" of 15:16 seems to count by long lifetimes: Moses was in the fourth generation from Levi (Exodus 6:16–20). The numbers matter for the debate over dating the Exodus, but they were not meant as a precise calendar.

a: for the guilt of the Amorites is not yet full
p: God delays giving the land until its people's sin is "full." Readers wrestle with what this says about the conquest.
b: The land is not given at once because the Amorites, a general name for the land's peoples, are not yet ripe for judgment. The verse presents the later conquest as God's justice on a people whose evil had grown over centuries (Leviticus 18:24–28; Deuteronomy 9:4–5), not as favoritism for Israel. It also shows patience: God waits four generations. Jewish and Christian readers have used the verse to explain the conquest and also to warn Israel that the same rule applies to them (Leviticus 18:28). Many modern readers find the conquest troubling however it is explained, and critical scholars see this as a later explanation of it.

a: a smoking oven and a blazing torch passed between these pieces
p: Only the fire, a sign of God's presence, passes between the pieces. Abram does not.
b: Smoke and fire mark God's presence: the pillar of cloud and fire (Exodus 13:21), the smoking mountain of Sinai (Exodus 19:18). In the rite of 15:10, the party who passes between the pieces takes the oath. Here only God passes, while Abram lies in a trance. Moshe Weinfeld compared this to royal "grants" in the ancient Near East, where a king bound himself to give land to a loyal servant, unlike treaties that bind a vassal. Many Christian theologians call this an unconditional covenant: its keeping depends on God alone. Others note that obedience is still expected (17:1; 18:19; 22:16–18).

a: the LORD cut a covenant with Abram
p: The Hebrew idiom for making a covenant is "cutting" one, maybe from rites like this one.
b: A berit, "covenant," is a binding agreement sworn by oath, between equals, between a king and vassal, or between God and people. Hebrew "cuts" a covenant, an idiom that may come from rites like 15:10. This is the first covenant God makes with Abram; the second, with circumcision as its sign, follows in chapter 17. God's covenant with Noah came before (9:9–17). The New Testament speaks of a "new covenant" in Jesus' blood (Luke 22:20; Hebrews 8:8–13) while Paul insists that the promise to Abraham still stands (Galatians 3:15–18).

a: from the river of Egypt to the great river, the river Euphrates
p: These are the largest borders the Bible gives the land. Israel held something like them only under David and Solomon.
b: Other passages give smaller borders, from Dan to Beersheba (Judges 20:1), or "the brook of Egypt," the Wadi el-Arish in the northern Sinai (Numbers 34:5). "The river of Egypt" here may mean the Nile or that same wadi. Only Solomon is said to rule from the Euphrates to the border of Egypt, and then over vassal kingdoms rather than settled land (1 Kings 4:21). Some modern religious nationalists have cited the verse to support a "Greater Israel"; most Jewish and Christian readers do not take it as a modern map. Christians often read the promise as widened in Christ to "the world" (Romans 4:13).

a: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites
p: This is the longest of the Bible's lists of the land's peoples: ten names instead of the usual six or seven.
b: Most lists name six or seven nations (Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1). This one has ten, perhaps to signal completeness. The first three are unusual. The Kenites were a clan of smiths related to Moses' in-laws (Judges 1:16; 4:11); Caleb was a Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12); "Kadmonites" means "Easterners." Rashi took the extra nations to be Edom, Moab and Ammon, whose land would be Israel's only in the age to come. The Hittites, Amorites and Jebusites appear later in the story (23:3; 14:13; 2 Samuel 5:6).
r: Exodus 3:8; Deuteronomy 7:1; Joshua 3:10; Judges 1:16; Numbers 32:12; Nehemiah 9:8

a: she owned a slave woman from Egypt named Hagar
p: An Egyptian slave woman becomes the mother of Ishmael. Jews, Christians and Muslims remember her very differently.
b: Hagar was probably acquired in Egypt (12:16); the Midrash made her Pharaoh's own daughter, given to Sarai after the plagues (Genesis Rabbah 45:1). She is the first person in the Bible visited by an angel and the only one who gives God a name (16:13). In Islam, Hajar is honored as the mother of Ishmael (Isma'il) and, through him, ancestress of the Prophet Muhammad; pilgrims at Mecca run seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa to remember her search for water (see 21:19). Paul uses her as an allegory of slavery under the Law (Galatians 4:21–31; see Genesis 21:10). Modern feminist and womanist readers, such as Phyllis Trible and Delores Williams, see in Hagar the story of every woman used, abused and cast out, whom God nonetheless sees.

a: Go in to my slave woman
p: Ancient laws and contracts let a childless wife give her slave to her husband. The child counted as hers.
b: Sarai's plan was legal and respectable in her world. The Laws of Hammurabi (about 1750 BC, sections 144–147) deal with a priestess-wife who gives her husband a slave woman to bear children, and forbid the slave to claim equal rank with her mistress. An Old Assyrian marriage contract from Kanesh in Turkey (about 1900 BC) says that if the wife has no child within two years she will buy a slave woman for her husband. Rachel and Leah do the same with their servants (30:3, 9). The child would legally belong to the wife, which is what Sarai means by "Maybe I can be built into a family through her."

a: Maybe I can be built into a family through her
p: Sarai's word "be built" sounds like the word for "son." She hopes to gain a son through Hagar.
b: Ibbaneh, "I will be built," comes from banah, "build," which sounds like ben, "son." A family in Hebrew is a "house," and children "build" it (Deuteronomy 25:9; Ruth 4:11, where Rachel and Leah "built the house of Israel"). Rachel uses the same words when she gives Bilhah to Jacob (30:3). Sarai's "maybe" is the only hope she has left.
orig: אִבָּנֶה מִמֶּנָּה (ibbaneh mimmennah), "I will be built from her"

a: And Abram listened to Sarai
p: Abram "listened to" his wife; she "took" and "gave" to her husband. The words recall Adam and Eve (3:6, 17).
b: God told Adam, "Since you obeyed your wife's voice..." (3:17), and Eve "took" the fruit and "gave" it to her husband (3:6). The narrator uses the same verbs here: Abram "listened to the voice of Sarai," and Sarai "took" Hagar and "gave" her to her husband (16:3). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, hear a quiet judgment: a human plan to get what God has promised. Later God himself tells Abraham to "listen to her" (21:12), which some take as a deliberate reversal.

a: her mistress became small in her eyes
p: The verb is the same root as "treat with contempt" in God's promise of 12:3.
b: Vatteqal means "she became light" or "small": once pregnant, Hagar no longer held Sarai in honor. It is the root qalal of 12:3, "whoever treats you with contempt." Proverbs 30:21–23 lists among things the earth cannot bear "a servant woman when she displaces her mistress." Sarai repeats the phrase word for word in her complaint (16:5).

a: So Sarai treated her harshly, and Hagar ran away from her
p: Sarai "afflicts" an Egyptian slave, the same verb used for Egypt afflicting Israel. Ramban called it a sin.
b: The verb 'anah, "afflict, oppress," is the word just used for what Egypt will do to Abram's offspring (15:13) and later for Israel's slavery (Exodus 1:11–12). Here the roles are reversed: an Egyptian slave woman is afflicted by Hebrews and flees, like Moses after her (Exodus 2:15). Ramban wrote that "our mother sinned in this affliction, and Abraham too, by allowing it," and that God heard Hagar's affliction (16:11) and gave her a son who would afflict Abraham's and Sarah's descendants. Rashi says only that Sarai worked her hard. Modern readers often see Abram's "do whatever seems good to you" as a failure to protect the mother of his child.

a: The angel of the LORD
p: The first appearance of "the angel of the LORD." He speaks as God himself, and Hagar names him as God.
b: A mal'akh is a messenger. "The angel of the LORD" speaks here in God's own voice ("I will multiply and multiply your offspring," 16:10), and Hagar names "the LORD who had spoken to her" (16:13). The same blurring between the angel and God appears at the binding of Isaac (22:11–16), at the burning bush (Exodus 3:2–6), and with Gideon (Judges 6:11–23). Jewish readers explain it as a messenger who speaks with God's authority, as an ambassador speaks for a king. Many early Christian writers, such as Justin Martyr, saw the Son of God appearing before his birth as a man. Many modern scholars think the "angel" was added to soften older stories in which God himself appeared.

a: the spring beside the road to Shur
p: Shur means "wall." Hagar is on the road home to Egypt.
b: Shur, "wall," was a desert region on Egypt's northeast frontier (25:18; Exodus 15:22; 1 Samuel 15:7). The name may come from the line of Egyptian border forts, called in Egyptian texts the "Walls of the Ruler," built about 2000 BC to keep out people from Canaan. Hagar, the Egyptian, is heading home. Kadesh (16:14) is the oasis of Kadesh-barnea in the northeastern Sinai, about 50 miles south of Beersheba.

a: Go back to your mistress, and bow yourself under her hand
p: The angel sends Hagar back to her abuser. Readers have found this one of the hardest verses in the story.
b: "Bow yourself" (hit'anni) is the same root as "mistreated" in 16:6: "let yourself be afflicted." Traditional readers explain that a pregnant woman alone in the desert would likely die, and that Ishmael needed to be born in Abram's house to be his acknowledged son (16:15). Some Christian writers saw a lesson in submission (compare 1 Peter 2:18). Womanist theologian Delores Williams argues that God's word to Hagar is about survival, not liberation: God helps her and her child live through an unjust situation, as he has helped many enslaved Black women. Either way, the command is followed at once by a promise (16:10).

a: I will multiply and multiply your offspring
p: Hagar is the only woman in the Bible to receive a promise of countless descendants in her own name.
b: God's promise to Hagar echoes his promise to Abram (13:16; 15:5) almost word for word, and is spoken to her directly. It comes true in the twelve tribes of Ishmael's sons (17:20; 25:12–16). Jewish and Christian tradition traced the Arab peoples to Ishmael (Josephus, Antiquities 1.214–221), and Muslims honor Ishmael's line as the family of the Prophet Muhammad.

a: Call him Ishmael, because the LORD has listened to your suffering
p: Ishmael means "God hears." The angel's words are the first of the Bible's birth announcements.
b: Yishma'el means "God hears." The pattern of this announcement, "you are pregnant (or will be), you will bear a son, you will name him...," returns for Samson's mother (Judges 13:3–5), in Isaiah's sign of Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14), and for Mary (Luke 1:31). "Misery" ('oni) is the word God uses for Israel's misery in Egypt, which he also "saw" and "heard" (Exodus 3:7). The name will be remembered when "God heard the boy's voice" in the desert (21:17).

a: He will be a wild donkey of a man
p: The onager is a symbol of untamed freedom in the Bible. Readers take the line as praise, warning, or both.
b: The pere' is the onager, the wild ass of the desert steppe, famous for roaming free and refusing to be tamed (Job 39:5–8; Jeremiah 2:24). Ishmael will be a free desert man, not a slave like his mother. "His hand against everyone" pictures a life of raids and fights. Older Christian and Jewish readers often took the verse as a hostile prophecy about the Arab peoples; many Muslim readers object that this reading turns a blessing into an insult. Most modern commentators read it as a picture of fierce independence. The Plain English keeps the literal "in the face of," which may mean "in defiance of," "alongside" or "to the east of" his brothers; 25:18 uses the same words of where his descendants settled.
orig: פֶּרֶא אָדָם (pere' adam), "a wild ass of a man"

a: You are El-roi, God who sees
p: Hagar is the only person in the Bible who gives God a name. The second half of the verse is very hard Hebrew.
b: El-ro'i can mean "God of seeing" or "God who sees me." The angel had said that the LORD "heard" (16:11); Hagar adds that he "sees." Her explanation is one of the hardest sentences in Genesis: literally "Have I even here seen after the one seeing me?" The Plain English keeps the plain sense of acharei, "after." Some modern commentators, Wenham among them, render "the back of" and compare Moses, who sees only God's back (Exodus 33:23), though "back" is a different Hebrew word there. Others read "Have I really gone on seeing here, after he saw me?" (so the KJV, NJPS and Alter in their own ways). Many modern scholars change one word to read "Have I really seen God and stayed alive after seeing him?" (see the variant).

a: Beer-lahai-roi
t: The well of the Living One who sees me
p: The name probably means "Well of the Living One who sees me." Isaac later lives there.
b: Be'er means "well," and the rest of the name is usually read "of the Living One who sees me" or "of the one who sees me and lives." The well was remembered in the Negev for generations. Isaac comes from there to meet Rebekah (24:62) and settles there after Abraham's death (25:11), so the two half-brothers' stories touch at Hagar's well. The site of Bered is unknown.

a: Abram was eighty-six
t: Eleven years of waiting, then thirteen of silence
p: Abram was 75 at the call and 86 at Ishmael's birth. Then Genesis jumps thirteen years.
b: The Priestly-style ages in this part of Genesis mark time: 75 at the call (12:4), ten years in Canaan before Sarai's plan (16:3), 86 at Ishmael's birth, and 99 when God speaks again (17:1). The narrator records no word from God for thirteen years. Jewish tradition and many Christian readers take the silence as a time when Abram assumed Ishmael was the promised heir (17:18).

a: I am God Almighty
p: "God Almighty" translates "El Shaddai," a name whose meaning is uncertain.
b: El Shaddai is the name God uses with the ancestors (28:3; 35:11; 48:3), and Exodus 6:3 says they knew him by it rather than by the name YHWH. Its meaning was lost early. Suggestions include "God of the mountain" (Akkadian shadu, "mountain"), "God of the breasts" (Hebrew shad), fitting the fertility promises that follow (compare "blessings of the breasts and of the womb," 49:25), and the rabbis' "the One who is sufficient" (she-dai; Rashi). "Almighty" comes through the Greek of Job (pantokrator) and the Latin omnipotens. In Genesis the Septuagint simply says "your God."

a: Go about your life in my sight, and be whole
p: "Tamim" means whole, complete, without defect. Noah was called the same.
b: Tamim describes an animal fit for sacrifice, "without defect" (Exodus 12:5), and a person of integrity: Noah was tamim (6:9), and Israel is told to be tamim with the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:13). It means wholeness more than sinless perfection: an undivided, sincere life. "Walk before me" pictures a servant living in his master's sight (compare 24:40; 48:15). The Midrash linked the word to circumcision: by removing the foreskin, Abraham would become "complete" (Genesis Rabbah 46:1). Jesus' "be perfect" (Matthew 5:48) may echo the same idea.
orig: הִתְהַלֵּךְ לְפָנַי וֶהְיֵה תָמִים (hithallekh lefanai veheyeh tamim)

a: Abraham will be your name
p: "Abram" means "exalted father." "Abraham" is explained by its sound: "father of a multitude."
b: Avram probably means "the father is exalted" or "exalted father." Avraham may once have been a longer form of the same name, but Genesis explains it by sound: av hamon, "father of a multitude" of nations. The rabbis taught that God added the letter he from his own name to Abram's, and the Talmud says that calling him "Abram" after this breaks a command (Berakhot 13a). The new name is a promise, since Abraham still has only one son. Paul quotes it: "I have made you the father of many nations," and says it means the father of all who believe (Romans 4:16–17). In Arabic the name is Ibrahim.

a: I will be God to you and to your offspring after you
p: This is the heart of every covenant in the Bible, and the last promise of Revelation.
b: The "covenant formula," "I will be your God and you will be my people," runs through the whole Bible: to Israel at the Exodus (Exodus 6:7), in the Law (Leviticus 26:12), in the promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27), in Paul (2 Corinthians 6:16), and at the very end, when "God himself will be with them and be their God" (Revelation 21:3). Here it is promised first to Abraham and his offspring. "For all time" ('olam) is the same word discussed at 13:15.
r: Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 31:33; Ezekiel 37:27; 2 Corinthians 6:16; Hebrews 8:10; Revelation 21:3

a: every male among you is to be circumcised
p: Many of Israel's neighbors practiced circumcision. Israel's version was given to infants, as a covenant sign.
b: Circumcision, cutting away the foreskin, was old and widespread. A relief in the tomb of Ankhmahor at Saqqara in Egypt (about 2300 BC) shows priests circumcising young men. The Greek historian Herodotus (400s BC) said Egyptians, Ethiopians and the "Syrians of Palestine" practiced it, and Jeremiah names Egypt, Edom, Ammon, Moab and the desert Arabs alongside Judah (Jeremiah 9:25–26). The Philistines, who came from the Aegean, did not, and "uncircumcised" became a byword for them (1 Samuel 17:26). What Genesis makes distinctive is timing and meaning: on the eighth day after birth, not at puberty or marriage, and as the sign of a covenant with God.

a: that will be the sign of the covenant between me and you
p: Jews keep circumcision as the covenant of Abraham. Paul argued that faith, not the sign, makes one a child of Abraham.
b: In Judaism, brit milah, "the covenant of circumcision," is performed on the eighth day even on the Sabbath (compare John 7:22–23), and the father blesses God "who commanded us to bring him into the covenant of Abraham our father." For the earliest church the question of whether Gentile believers must be circumcised was the first great dispute; the council in Jerusalem said no (Acts 15). Paul called circumcision "a seal of the righteousness" Abraham had by faith before he was circumcised (Romans 4:11), and spoke of a "circumcision of the heart" (Romans 2:28–29), an idea already in the Law and the prophets (Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4). Many Reformed Christians see baptism as its counterpart (Colossians 2:11–12), a reason they baptize infants. In Islam, circumcision (khitan) is a practice traced to Abraham; a hadith in al-Bukhari says he circumcised himself at the age of eighty.
r: Romans 4:9–12; Romans 2:28–29; Galatians 5:2–6; Acts 15:1–21; Colossians 2:11–12; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4

a: circumcised at eight days old
p: The Law repeats the eighth-day rule. Jesus and Paul were both circumcised on the eighth day.
b: Leviticus 12:3 repeats the command. Isaac is the first child circumcised on the eighth day (21:4). Luke records that Jesus was circumcised and named on the eighth day (Luke 2:21), and Paul lists "circumcised on the eighth day" first among his Jewish credentials (Philippians 3:5). The covenant sign was also given to slaves and foreigners in the household (17:12–13, 27), so from the start Abraham's household was not defined by blood alone. Josephus notes that the Arabs of his day circumcised at age thirteen, after the example of Ishmael (17:25).

a: will be cut off from his people
p: To be "cut off" is the penalty of the covenant. Scholars debate whether it means exile or death sent by God.
b: There is a grim wordplay: Israel "cuts" (karat) a covenant, and the man who refuses its sign will be "cut off" (nikhretah). The phrase recurs in the Law for serious sins (Exodus 12:15; Leviticus 7:20; 20:17). The rabbis understood karet as a penalty carried out by God, an early death or dying without children, rather than by a human court. Others think it meant being expelled from the community. Since an infant cannot circumcise himself, the duty falls on the parents (Exodus 4:24–26).

a: Sarah will be her name
p: Both names mean "princess." The change marks her as the promised mother of kings.
b: Sarai and Sarah are probably two forms of one word, "princess." The rabbis said that Sarai meant "my princess," princess to Abraham alone, and Sarah "princess" to all (Berakhot 13a). What matters is that God himself renames her, as he did Abraham, and promises her by name. She is the only woman in the Bible renamed by God, and she is told she will become nations and the mother of kings (17:16). Isaiah later calls Israel to "Look at Abraham your father, and at Sarah who gave you birth" (Isaiah 51:2).

a: Abraham fell on his face and laughed
p: Abraham laughs, and the boy will be called Isaac, "he laughs." Was it joy or doubt?
b: Abraham bows in worship and laughs at the same moment. Vayyitschaq, "and he laughed," is the verb behind Yitschaq, Isaac. Laughter returns again and again: Sarah laughs (18:12), Sarah says God has given her laughter (21:6), Ishmael is "laughing" (21:9), and Isaac "laughs" with Rebekah (26:8). The Aramaic Targum Onkelos translated Abraham's laugh as "rejoiced," and Rashi explained that Abraham laughed for joy while Sarah laughed in disbelief. Paul says Abraham "looked at his own body, which was dead," yet "his faith did not grow weak" (Romans 4:19). Many modern readers hear honest disbelief mixed with wonder.

a: As for Ishmael, I have heard you
p: "I have heard you" is a pun on Ishmael's name. He will have twelve chiefs, as Jacob will have twelve sons.
b: God answers Abraham's prayer for Ishmael (17:18) with a pun: shema'tikha, "I have heard you," sounds like Yishma'el, "God hears." Ishmael receives nearly every blessing Abraham does: fruitfulness, many descendants, a great nation. His twelve "chiefs" (nesi'im) are listed in 25:13–16, a match for the twelve tribes of Israel. What he does not receive is the covenant (17:21).

a: But my covenant I will keep in force with Isaac
p: Genesis passes the covenant to Isaac, not Ishmael. Islam honors both sons as prophets.
b: God blesses Ishmael but sets his covenant with Isaac, a son not yet conceived. Jewish and Christian tradition follow Genesis: the covenant line runs through Isaac and Jacob (Romans 9:7–9, quoting Genesis 21:12). Islam tells the story another way. The Qur'an honors Ishmael (Isma'il) as a prophet and messenger who helped Abraham build the Kaaba (Qur'an 2:125–129; 19:54–55), and honors Isaac as a prophet too (37:112–113). Muslims trace the Prophet Muhammad's line to Ishmael. Genesis itself keeps both sons in view: they bury their father together (25:9).

a: That very day
p: Abraham obeys on the same day, as he will rise early to obey in 22:3.
b: "That very day" (be'etsem hayyom hazzeh) is the phrase Genesis uses for Noah entering the ark (7:13), and the Law uses for the Exodus (Exodus 12:41). Abraham, ninety-nine, circumcises himself, his son and every male of his household at once. His prompt obedience returns when he rises early to take Isaac to Moriah (22:3). Ishmael, at thirteen, is the first son to receive the sign, ahead of Isaac.

a: The LORD appeared to Abraham
p: The LORD appears, and Abraham sees three men. Jews, Christians and Muslims have read the scene in different ways.
b: The narrator tells us first that "the LORD appeared," then that Abraham saw "three men." Later the LORD stays with Abraham while "the men" go toward Sodom (18:22), and two "angels" arrive there (19:1). Jewish tradition says the three were angels, each with one task: Michael to announce Isaac's birth, Gabriel to overturn Sodom, Raphael to heal Abraham (Bava Metzia 86b; Rashi). Many early Christian writers, such as Justin Martyr, said one was the Son of God and two were angels; others saw a hint of the Trinity, made famous by Andrei Rublev's icon (about 1420). Hebrews draws a simpler lesson: "some, without realizing it, have had angels as guests" (Hebrews 13:2). The Qur'an tells of Abraham's "honored guests," messengers who come with news of Isaac and of Lot's people (Qur'an 11:69–76; 51:24–37).

a: in the heat of the day
p: The rabbis noticed that this visit comes right after Abraham's circumcision, and drew a lesson.
b: Since the last chapter ended with Abraham's circumcision, the rabbis said God came on the third day after it to visit him while he was sore, and that is why the LORD "appeared" before any message is given. From this they taught that visiting the sick is a way of imitating God: "As he visited the sick, so you visit the sick" (Sotah 14a; Bava Metzia 86b). They added that God made the day hot so no travelers would trouble Abraham, but Abraham sat at his door, hoping for guests to welcome anyway.

a: My lord
p: The Hebrew can be read as a polite "my lord" to a guest, or as "Lord," spoken to God. The Masoretes chose "Lord."
b: The consonants 'dny can be read adoni, "my lord," a polite address to a man, or Adonai, "Lord," the word used for God. The Masoretic vowels give the divine form, treating it as holy. The Talmud records both views (Shevuot 35b). On one reading Abraham turns to God and says, "Lord, please do not leave," while he runs to serve his guests. From this the rabbis drew a famous saying: "Welcoming guests is greater than receiving the presence of God" (Shabbat 127a). Most modern translations read "my lord," spoken to the leader of the three.

a: wash your feet
p: Water for the feet, shade, bread: Abraham offers the full courtesy of the desert, and then far more.
b: In a hot land where people walked in sandals, water for washing the feet was the first gift to a guest (19:2; 24:32; Judges 19:21). Jesus rebukes a host who gave him none (Luke 7:44) and washes his disciples' feet himself (John 13:4–14). Abraham's words are modest, "a little water," "a bit of bread," but what he serves is a feast. Among the herding peoples of the Near East, protecting and feeding strangers was a sacred duty, which is why the contrast with Sodom in the next chapter is so sharp.

a: Three measures of the best flour
p: Three seahs would make bread for dozens. Jesus' parable of the yeast uses the same amount.
b: A se'ah was a dry measure, often estimated at about 7 liters (some estimates are larger), so three seahs is about 20 liters, over 5 gallons of flour: bread for a crowd, not three guests. Abraham's generosity runs wild. Jesus' parable of the woman who hid yeast "in three measures of flour" (Matthew 13:33; Luke 13:21) uses the same quantity, which some interpreters think recalls this meal. Gideon also prepares an ephah of flour, about the same amount, for the angel of the LORD (Judges 6:19).

a: He stood beside them under the tree while they ate
p: Genesis says the visitors ate. The rabbis and the Qur'an say they only seemed to.
b: Abraham stands like a servant while his guests eat. That heavenly beings ate a meal troubled later readers. The Talmud says they only appeared to eat, out of courtesy: "When you go to a town, follow its customs" (Bava Metzia 86b). The book of Tobit has the angel Raphael say, "Now you see that I never ate anything; you were seeing a vision" (Tobit 12:19). In the Qur'an, the guests' hands do not reach for the roasted calf, and Abraham becomes afraid of them (Qur'an 11:70; 51:26–28). Many Christian writers took the text plainly: the risen Jesus also ate to show he was real (Luke 24:42–43). Jewish readers also noted the meat with milk, later forbidden together; Rashi says Abraham served each dish as it was ready.

a: They asked him
p: In Hebrew scrolls three letters of "to him" carry dots above them. The rabbis read a hidden meaning.
b: In the Masoretic Text the word elav, "to him," has dots over three of its letters, one of ten places in the Torah marked this way. The dots probably once showed that a scribe doubted the letters. The rabbis read them as a hint: the dotted letters spell ayyo, "where is he?", so the angels also asked Sarah where Abraham was, teaching that a guest should ask after both host and hostess (Bava Metzia 87a; Rashi). The dots do not change the plain meaning.
orig: אֵלָיו (elav), with dots over א, י, ו

a: when the season comes round again
p: Elisha later uses the same promise for a childless woman of Shunem, and Paul quotes this verse.
b: The phrase ka'et chayyah, literally "at the time of life" or "as the time revives," seems to mean "when this season comes round next year." Elisha uses the same words to a childless woman: "At this set time, when the season comes round again," she will have a son (2 Kings 4:16–17). Paul quotes the promise to show that Isaac was a child of God's word, not of natural strength: "At this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son" (Romans 9:9).

a: After I am worn out, will I have pleasure, and my lord old too?
p: Sarah laughs at the idea of pleasure at her age. Peter later quotes her calling Abraham "my lord."
b: "Worn out" is the word for clothing that has worn thin (Deuteronomy 8:4). "Pleasure," 'ednah, is related to Eden and means delight, here plainly sexual delight and its fruit. Sarah's laugh is inward, "inside herself," yet the LORD hears it. Peter cites Sarah as a model wife "who obeyed Abraham and called him lord" (1 Peter 3:6), quoting this very private line. Hebrews may count her among the faithful: "by faith even Sarah received strength to found a family" (Hebrews 11:11), though many scholars read the Greek as speaking of Abraham's faith, with Sarah named only as barren.

a: Can I truly bear a child, when I am this old?
p: Sarah thought "my lord old too." God reports her as saying "when I am this old." The rabbis saw a lesson about peace.
b: When the LORD repeats Sarah's words to Abraham, he leaves out "my lord old too" and says only "when I am this old." The rabbis noticed the change and taught: "Great is peace, for even the Holy One changed the truth for its sake" (Yevamot 65b; Bava Metzia 87a; Rashi). This became the classic text in Jewish ethics for when one may soften the truth to keep peace in a family. Others simply see God answering the doubt at the heart of her words.

a: Is anything too wonderful for the LORD?
p: The question returns in Jeremiah and in the angel's words to Mary.
b: The verb pala' means "to be extraordinary, beyond human power," the root of the word for God's "wonders." Jeremiah prays, "Nothing is too hard for you," and God answers, "Is anything too wonderful for me?" (Jeremiah 32:17, 27). The angel Gabriel tells Mary, after announcing that her old relative Elizabeth is pregnant, "no word that comes from God will be powerless" (Luke 1:37), wording close to the Septuagint of this verse. Both stories tie a miraculous birth to God's power alone.

a: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?
p: God shares his plans with Abraham, as with a friend. Abraham is called "God's friend" in Isaiah, James and the Qur'an.
b: God talks with himself about whether to tell Abraham. "The Lord GOD does nothing unless he first reveals his plan to his servants the prophets" (Amos 3:7). Jesus says, "I have called you friends, because all I heard from my Father I have let you know" (John 15:15). Abraham is the only person called God's "friend" (ohev) in the Hebrew Bible (Isaiah 41:8; 2 Chronicles 20:7), and James repeats the title (James 2:23). In Islam he is Khalil Allah, "the intimate friend of God" (Qur'an 4:125), and Hebron is called al-Khalil in Arabic after him.

a: I have chosen him
p: "Know" here means "choose." And the purpose of the choosing is justice.
b: Yada', "know," can mean to choose someone for a close relationship: "Of all the clans of the earth, you alone have I known" (Amos 3:2); "I knew you before I shaped you in the womb" (Jeremiah 1:5). God's choice has a purpose: that Abraham teach his household "the way of the LORD by doing what is right and just" (tsedaqah umishpat). The pair returns in the prophets (Isaiah 5:7; Jeremiah 22:15) and comes just before the case of Sodom, where justice is the question. Jewish tradition often names tsedaqah, which came to mean "charity," as Abraham's legacy to his children.

a: The outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah is great
p: "Outcry" is the scream of people being wronged. The word points to Sodom's sin: cruelty to the weak.
b: Za'aqah (and its twin tse'aqah, 18:21) is the cry of the oppressed for help: Israel's cry in Egypt (Exodus 3:7–9), the cry of the widow and orphan (Exodus 22:22–23), and Isaiah's pun on the vineyard that bore "a cry" instead of "righteousness" (Isaiah 5:7). So the outcry "against" Sodom is most likely the cry of its victims. Ezekiel names both kinds of sin: "This was the sin of Sodom your sister: pride, more food than they needed, and easy comfort, yet she did not help the poor and needy. They grew proud and did a detestable thing before me" (Ezekiel 16:49–50). The rabbis told stories of Sodom's laws against charity, including a girl punished for secretly feeding a beggar, whose cry rose to heaven (Sanhedrin 109b; Genesis Rabbah 49:6). Chapter 19 shows the city's violence toward strangers.
orig: זַעֲקַת סְדֹם (za'aqat sedom), "the cry of Sodom"

a: I will go down and see
p: As at Babel, God "goes down" to look before judging. The rabbis took it as a lesson for judges.
b: God "came down to see" the tower of Babel before acting (11:5–7), and later "came down" to rescue Israel from Egypt (Exodus 3:8). The words are not about God's lack of knowledge, the rabbis said, but a model for human judges: never condemn without seeing the evidence for yourself (Rashi, following the Midrash). The phrase "If not, I will know" leaves room for mercy.

a: Will you really sweep away the righteous along with the wicked?
p: Abraham bargains with God for a city. Jews treasure the right to argue with God; Christians see bold intercession.
b: Abraham does not ask God to spare Lot by name. He argues for a principle: the innocent should not die with the guilty, and the presence of the righteous can save a city. Jewish tradition sees here the first great example of arguing with God for justice, followed by Moses (Exodus 32:11–14), Job and the prophets, and in modern times by writers such as Elie Wiesel. The Midrash has Abraham say, "If you want a world, there cannot be strict justice; if you want strict justice, there can be no world" (Genesis Rabbah 49:9). Christian readers see a model of intercession: "a righteous person's prayer can do much" (James 5:16), and some point to Christ, the one righteous man for whose sake many are spared (Romans 5:19).
r: Exodus 32:11–14; Numbers 14:13–19; Jeremiah 5:1; Ezekiel 14:14; James 5:16; Romans 5:18–19

a: Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?
t: The Judge of all the earth
p: Abraham appeals to God's own character. Paul and the Psalms echo the question.
b: Abraham holds God to his own standard: mishpat, justice, the word God used in 18:19. "Judge of all the earth" makes God the judge not only of Israel but of every city, including a Canaanite one. The Psalms call on him by the same title (Psalm 94:2; 96:13), and Paul asks, if God were unjust, "how will God judge the world?" (Romans 3:5–6). The question is also the root of the Bible's long debate about suffering, carried on in Job and Habakkuk (Habakkuk 1:13).

a: though I am only dust and ashes
p: "Afar va'efer" is a rhyming phrase for the frailty of human beings.
b: 'Afar va'efer, "dust and ashes," rhymes in Hebrew. Dust recalls that Adam was made of dust and returns to it (2:7; 3:19); ashes suggest mourning and what is left after fire, like the fire about to fall on Sodom. Job uses the same pair twice (Job 30:19; 42:6). Abraham's humility and his boldness grow together: the more he presses God, the lower he bows.

a: Suppose ten are found there
p: Abraham stops at ten. Readers have long asked why.
b: Abraham bargains from fifty down to ten and then stops, and God goes away. Rashi suggested that Abraham knew that Noah's family, eight people, had not been enough to save the world in the flood, so he did not go below ten. Ten later became the number needed for public prayer in Judaism, the minyan, though the Talmud bases that on other verses. Jeremiah goes much further: God would pardon Jerusalem if one person could be found who acts justly (Jeremiah 5:1). Some readers think Abraham stops because he assumes Lot's household alone would make ten; it does not, and the next chapter shows what happens instead: God rescues the few rather than sparing the city.

a: Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom
p: The city gate was where elders met and judged. Lot, the outsider, has become a man of standing.
