b: In ancient towns the gate was more than a doorway: it was the square where business was done, deals were witnessed and cases were judged (23:10; Ruth 4:1–11; Deuteronomy 21:19). To "sit in the gate" suggests Lot had become a leading man of Sodom. The men of the city resent exactly this: "This one came here to live as a foreigner, and now he keeps playing judge!" (19:9). Gates of the Middle Bronze Age, with chambers and benches inside them, have been excavated at Dan, Gezer and other sites.

a: we will spend the night in the town square
p: Judges 19 tells a story so close to this one that one seems to be modeled on the other.
b: In Judges 19 a Levite and his concubine are about to spend the night in the square of Gibeah, in Israel, until an old man, himself an outsider in the town, takes them in. The men of the city surround the house and demand to "know" the guest; the host offers his daughter and the concubine; the concubine is raped through the night and dies (Judges 19:15–28). Many scholars think the writer of Judges deliberately echoes Sodom to say that Israel itself had become Sodom. In Judges no angels come to the rescue, and the result is civil war.

a: baked bread without yeast
p: A meal of unleavened bread, a night of judgment, a hurried escape at dawn: the scene foreshadows the Exodus.
b: Matsot are flat loaves made quickly without yeast, the bread of haste and of Passover (Exodus 12:8, 39). Rashi says the visit happened at Passover. Whether or not that was meant, the pattern is there: a household shelters inside a door while death passes through the city (Exodus 12:22–23), the family is hurried out at dawn, and they must not look back or linger. Lot's meal is simpler than Abraham's feast (18:6–8), but it is still real hospitality, the only kind in Sodom.

a: so we can know them
p: "Know" is a common Hebrew way to say "have sex with." Here it means a demand for gang rape.
b: Yada', "know," often means sexual intercourse in Hebrew (4:1; 4:25), and Lot answers by offering daughters who "have not known a man" (19:8). In 1955 Derrick Sherwin Bailey argued that here it meant only "get acquainted with," a demand to check the strangers' papers; few scholars accept that, since Lot's reply makes the sexual sense plain. What the crowd demands is the gang rape of two guests, a violent attempt to humiliate outsiders. The same verb is used in the Gibeah story (Judges 19:22).
orig: וְנֵדְעָה אֹתָם (vened'ah otam), "and let us know them"

a: Bring them out to us
t: What was the sin of Sodom?
p: Sodom's sin has been named as violence, inhospitality, pride, injustice or same-sex acts. The Bible names several.
b: Genesis has already called the outcry "great" (18:20). Ezekiel lists "pride, more food than they needed, and easy comfort," with no help for the poor, and goes on: "they grew proud and did a detestable thing (to'evah) before me" (Ezekiel 16:49–50). Traditional interpreters, and modern ones such as Robert Gagnon, link that word to Leviticus 18:22 and 20:13, where it names sex between men. Jubilees (16:5–6; 20:5) and the Testament of Naphtali (3:4–5), which compares Sodom with the Watchers of 6:1–4, stress sexual sin; Jude says the cities "gave themselves to sexual immorality and went after other flesh" (Jude 7), and 2 Peter speaks of their "unbridled conduct" (2 Peter 2:7). Philo, Josephus and the Qur'an (7:80–81) single out men's lust for men. Others stress hospitality: Jesus links Sodom with towns that refuse to welcome his messengers (Matthew 10:14–15), Wisdom blames hatred of strangers (Wisdom 19:13–15), and Isaiah names injustice (Isaiah 1:10–17). Traditional Jewish, Christian and Muslim teaching sees same-sex acts as at least part of the sin; many modern scholars argue the story condemns gang rape and cruelty to strangers, not loving same-sex relationships. All agree the scene shows a city that preys on the vulnerable.
r: 18:20–21; Ezekiel 16:49–50; Leviticus 18:22; Isaiah 1:10–17; Jude 7; 2 Peter 2:6–10; Matthew 10:14–15

a: Let me bring them out to you
p: Lot protects his guests by offering his own daughters. No reader, ancient or modern, finds this easy.
b: Lot holds to the duty of protecting guests "under the shelter of my roof," but sacrifices his daughters to do it. Some ancient readers praised his hospitality and saw an offer he never expected the crowd to accept. The Midrash condemned him: a father should fight to the death for his daughters, and Lot offered them up (Tanhuma Vayera 12; compare Genesis Rabbah 50:7). Modern readers, especially feminist scholars, see the story as showing how little women counted in that world, and note that the narrator never approves. The angels' rescue makes the offer unnecessary. 2 Peter 2:7–8 calls Lot "righteous," distressed by the lawless people around him; readers have long felt the tension between that verdict and this scene.

a: This one came here to live as a foreigner, and now he keeps playing judge!
p: The crowd's insult uses the words "ger" (foreigner) and "judge." Lot is still an outsider in Sodom.
b: "Came to live as a foreigner" is the verb gur (see 12:10): after years in Sodom, Lot is still a ger, a resident outsider, to its people. "He keeps on judging" (vayyishpot shafot) mocks his seat in the gate (19:1) and his attempt to tell them what is evil (19:7). The scene asks the same question as 18:25, "Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?" Lot is a poor judge; God is about to judge in earnest.
orig: הָאֶחָד בָּא־לָגוּר וַיִּשְׁפֹּט שָׁפוֹט (ha'echad ba-lagur vayyishpot shafot)

a: with blindness
p: The rare word "sanverim" means a dazzling blindness sent by heaven. It appears only here and in 2 Kings 6.
b: Sanverim is not the ordinary word for blindness. It appears only here and in 2 Kings 6:18, where God strikes an Aramean army at Elisha's prayer so they cannot recognize where they are. Many think it comes from a word meaning "dazzling light." The men are not left permanently blind but confused, groping for a door they cannot find. In both stories the blinding protects God's servants from a mob.

a: his sons-in-law thought he was joking
p: "Joking" is the verb behind Isaac's name. Lot's warning is a joke to his family.
b: Metsacheq, "joking, laughing," comes from tsachaq, the verb of Abraham's and Sarah's laughter (17:17; 18:12) and of Isaac's name. Here the laugh is unbelief in judgment, not in promise. The same word returns for Ishmael "playing" (21:9) and Isaac "laughing with" Rebekah (26:8). Whether these men were already married to Lot's daughters or only engaged is debated; most take them as engaged, since the daughters "have not known a man" (19:8). Jesus warned that the coming of the Son of Man would be like the days of Lot, when people went on with life until the fire fell (Luke 17:28–30).

a: because the LORD had pity on him
p: Lot drags his feet, and the angels pull him out by the hand. The rescue is mercy, not merit.
b: Lot "lingered," the verb used of people who hesitate when they should hurry (43:10; Exodus 12:39). The angels take him and his family by the hand. The narrator says why: chemlah, "pity, compassion," from the LORD. 19:29 adds that God "remembered Abraham." 2 Peter 2:9 draws the lesson: "the Lord knows how to rescue the devout from testing and to hold the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment." Lot is saved because of God's mercy and Abraham's prayer, not because of his own courage.

a: That is why the town was named Zoar
p: Lot keeps calling the town "little" (mits'ar), which explains its name Zoar.
b: Lot twice calls the town mits'ar, "only a small one" (19:20), and the narrator explains its name, Tso'ar, from the same root. Its old name was Bela (14:2). Zoar was remembered at the southeast end of the Dead Sea (Deuteronomy 34:3; Isaiah 15:5), and a town of that name existed there in Roman and Byzantine times, near modern Ghor es-Safi in Jordan. The point of the pun: Lot pleads that a small sin city is not worth destroying, and God grants it.

a: from the LORD, out of the sky
p: The verse names the LORD twice. Early Christians saw the Father and the Son; most others see a Hebrew way of emphasis.
b: "The LORD rained... from the LORD, out of the sky." Justin Martyr and many early church writers took the doubled name as a sign of two divine persons: the Son on earth, who had spoken with Abraham, raining fire from the Father in heaven (Justin, Dialogue with Trypho 56, 129). The Council of Sirmium (AD 351) made it a test of orthodoxy to read the verse this way. Jewish interpreters and most modern scholars read it as emphatic repetition, the narrator underlining that the fire came straight from God, as in Hebrew poetry or law (compare 1 Kings 8:1). Rashi notes that Scripture often repeats a name instead of saying "from himself."

a: sulfur and fire
p: Some see an earthquake and burning bitumen; others a meteor airburst. Archaeologists disagree on where Sodom was.
b: The Dead Sea lies on a major fault line, its valley is rich in bitumen, sulfur and natural gas, and earthquakes there have ignited fires; many have suggested such a disaster as the memory behind the story. Two locations are argued. In the south, the Early Bronze Age towns of Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira, near the Lisan peninsula, show destruction or abandonment in the Early Bronze Age (Numeira about 2600–2550 BC, Bab edh-Dhra later, about 2350 BC, on the excavators' dates), earlier than most dates for Abraham. In the north, Steven Collins identifies Sodom with Tall el-Hammam, northeast of the Dead Sea; a 2021 paper in Scientific Reports by Ted Bunch and colleagues argued that a cosmic airburst destroyed it about 1650 BC, but other scientists have strongly challenged the study's evidence. Critical scholars often think the story grew from the eerie, salt-crusted landscape itself. The Bible calls it simply an act of God.

a: He overthrew those cities
p: "Overthrow" became the Bible's set word for Sodom's fate, used by Moses, the prophets and Jesus.
b: The verb hafakh, "overturn, overthrow," and its noun mahpekhah (19:29) are used for Sodom again and again: "like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim" (Deuteronomy 29:23); "I overthrew some of you, as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah" (Amos 4:11; compare Isaiah 1:9; 13:19; Jeremiah 49:18; 50:40). Jesus says the towns that reject his messengers will be worse off on judgment day than Sodom (Matthew 10:15; 11:23–24), and Revelation says the great city "where their Lord was also crucified" is "symbolically called Sodom and Egypt" (Revelation 11:8).
r: Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 1:9; Isaiah 13:19; Jeremiah 49:18; Amos 4:11; Lamentations 4:6; Matthew 10:15; Matthew 11:23–24; Revelation 11:8

a: she turned into a pillar of salt
p: Salt pillars still stand on Mount Sodom by the Dead Sea. Jesus said, "Remember Lot's wife."
b: Lot's wife is never named; later Jewish tradition calls her Idit or Edith (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 25). The Midrash says she was punished "with salt" because she would not share salt with guests (Genesis Rabbah 51:5). On Mount Sodom (Jebel Usdum), a ridge of rock salt at the southwest of the Dead Sea, erosion carves pillars, and one has long been called "Lot's wife." The Wisdom of Solomon (10:7) and Josephus (Antiquities 1.203) both say her pillar could still be seen in their day. Jesus used her as a warning against clinging to the old life when judgment comes: "Remember Lot's wife" (Luke 17:31–33). The Qur'an also says Lot's wife was among those left behind (Qur'an 11:81; 66:10).

a: like the smoke of a kiln
p: The same rare word, "kivshan," describes Mount Sinai smoking when God came down.
b: A kivshan is a kiln or smelting furnace. The word appears again at Sinai, "since the LORD had come down upon it in the fire. Its smoke went up like a furnace's smoke" (Exodus 19:18). God's presence and God's judgment are pictured by the same fire. Revelation uses the image of rising smoke for judgment on Babylon: "her smoke goes up forever and ever" (Revelation 19:3; compare Revelation 14:11; 9:2). Abraham stands where he had pleaded and sees that not even ten were found.
r: Exodus 19:18; Revelation 9:2; Revelation 14:11; Revelation 18:9; Revelation 19:3; Isaiah 34:9–10

a: he remembered Abraham
p: "God remembered" Noah in the flood; now he remembers Abraham. Lot is saved for his uncle's sake.
b: When God "remembers" in the Bible, he acts on a commitment: "God remembered Noah" and the waters went down (8:1); "God remembered Rachel" and opened her womb (30:22); "God remembered his covenant with Abraham" and began the Exodus (Exodus 2:24). This verse sums up the chapter in the style of the Priestly writer: God did not spare the city, but he answered the heart of Abraham's prayer by rescuing the righteous man inside it. Lot is saved for Abraham's sake.

a: there is no man in the land to come in to us
p: The daughters may have thought the whole world was destroyed. Readers have judged them harshly and kindly.
b: The daughters fear their father's family line will end. Some Jewish readers defended them: they thought the whole world had been burned, as in Noah's flood, and acted to keep humanity alive (Genesis Rabbah 51:8; Rashi). Others saw sin and shame. The story echoes Noah, who also became drunk after a world-ending disaster and was shamed by his child (9:20–25). Critical scholars once read it as an Israelite insult against Moab and Ammon; others think it may come from those peoples' own story of a heroic ancestress. The narrator gives no verdict. Lot, who offered his daughters to the crowd, is now used by them; some readers see a grim kind of justice.

a: He did not know when she lay down or when she got up
p: In Hebrew scrolls the word "when she got up" has a dot over one letter on the first night only.
b: The Masoretic Text places a dot over the vav of uvqumah, "and when she got up," in 19:33, but not in the same phrase in 19:35. The rabbis read the dot as a hint that Lot did become aware afterward, the first night, and so was to blame for drinking again the second night (Genesis Rabbah 51:8; Nazir 23a; Rashi). Text scholars think such dots once marked doubtful letters. See also the dots at 18:9.
orig: וּבְקוּמָהּ (uvqumah), with a dot over the ו

a: He is the ancestor of the Moabites to this day
t: Moab, Ammon and the line of David
p: Moab and Ammon were Israel's kin and rivals. From both came mothers of Israel's kings.
b: "Moab" sounds like me'av, "from father," and "Ben-ammi" means "son of my kin." The Law kept Moabites and Ammonites out of the LORD's assembly for ten generations (Deuteronomy 23:3–6), yet also forbade Israel to take their land, "for I have given it to the descendants of Lot" (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19). From Moab came Ruth, great-grandmother of David (Ruth 4:13–22), and from Ammon came Naamah, mother of King Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:21). The Talmud speaks of "two good doves," Ruth and Naamah, brought out of this dark night (Bava Kamma 38b). Matthew names Ruth in the family line of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
r: Deuteronomy 2:9; Deuteronomy 2:19; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Ruth 4:13–22; 1 Kings 14:21; Matthew 1:5

a: While he was staying as a foreigner in Gerar
p: Gerar lay in the western Negev, probably at Tel Haror. Abraham is again an outsider in a foreign king's land.
b: Gerar is usually identified with Tel Haror (Tell Abu Hureira), about 12 miles northwest of Beersheba on the Wadi Gerar, a large city in the Middle Bronze Age. "Between Kadesh and Shur" places Abraham's wanderings in the dry country between the Sinai and southern Canaan (compare 16:7, 14). Isaac later lives in Gerar too, with the same king's name, Abimelech, and the same trouble over a wife (26:1–11). On why the king is later called a Philistine, see 21:32.

a: She is another man's wife
p: The Hebrew phrase for "married woman" is "one mastered by a master," using the word "baal."
b: Be'ulat ba'al means literally "one possessed by a lord (husband)": ba'al is the word for owner, master, husband, and the name of the Canaanite god Baal. The same phrase appears in the law against adultery (Deuteronomy 22:22). Egyptian marriage contracts and texts from Ugarit call adultery "the great sin" (compare "such great guilt," 20:9; Moran and Rabinowitz, 1959), and God's warning treats taking another man's wife as a crime worthy of death, even for a king who did not know. God speaks in dreams to non-Israelites in Genesis: Abimelech, Laban (31:24) and Pharaoh (41:1–7).

a: will you kill a nation even if it is innocent?
t: The foreign king argues like Abraham
p: Abimelech asks God Abraham's own question from Sodom: will you kill the righteous?
b: "Innocent" is tsaddiq, "righteous," the word Abraham used when he pleaded for Sodom: "Will you really sweep away the righteous along with the wicked?" (18:23–25). Now a foreign king asks it about himself, and God agrees with him (20:6). "A clear heart and clean hands" (20:5) is the language of the psalms for a person fit to stand before God (Psalm 24:4; 26:6). The story turns the tables again: the pagan is righteous, and the prophet is the one who has put others in danger.

a: He is a prophet, and he will pray for you
p: Abraham is the first person called a "prophet" in the Bible, and the first who "prays" for someone.
b: A navi', "prophet," was a spokesman for God and also one who could plead with God for others: Moses (Numbers 21:7), Samuel (1 Samuel 12:23), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:16). This is the first use of both "prophet" and the verb "pray" (hitpallel) in the Bible. The Psalms remember the ancestors as God's "anointed ones" and "prophets" whom kings were not to harm (Psalm 105:14–15). The Qur'an too calls Abraham "a man of truth, a prophet" (Qur'an 19:41).
orig: נָבִיא הוּא וְיִתְפַּלֵּל בַּעַדְךָ (navi' hu veyitpallel ba'adkha)

a: There is no fear of God at all in this place
p: Abraham assumed foreigners had no conscience. Abimelech and his servants prove him wrong.
b: "The fear of God" in Genesis means moral conscience, the restraint that keeps people from murder and adultery even when no one would stop them (42:18; Exodus 1:17). Abraham assumed Gerar had none, but the king's men "were terrified" at God's warning (20:8). The phrase returns at the climax of Abraham's life, when the angel says, "Now I know that you fear God" (22:12). Rabbinic and Christian readers alike draw the lesson that God's people should not assume outsiders are without conscience.

a: she is in fact my sister, my father's daughter
p: Abraham says Sarah was his half-sister. Later law forbade such a marriage; Jewish tradition said she was his niece.
b: Marriage to a half-sister was later forbidden in Israel's law (Leviticus 18:9, 11; 20:17; Ezekiel 22:11), though Tamar's words to Amnon suggest it might once have been allowed (2 Samuel 13:13). Genesis never names Sarah's parents, and 11:29 lists her without them. Jewish tradition identified Sarah with Iscah, daughter of Abraham's brother Haran (11:29), so that "sister" meant a close relative, as Lot is called Abraham's "brother" (14:14; Megillah 14a; Rashi). Many modern readers think Abraham is offering a half-truth to save face. Traditional Christian readers took him at his word, noting that the Law came later.

a: When God sent me wandering
p: The verb with "God" here is plural, which is unusual. The Targum softened the line.
b: Normally Elohim meaning the one God takes a singular verb. Here the verb hit'u, "caused to wander," is plural. Some scholars think Abraham is speaking to a foreigner in the language of "the gods"; others note that Elohim sometimes takes plural verbs (35:7; 2 Samuel 7:23). The word "wander" can also mean "go astray," and the Aramaic Targum, uneasy with God leading Abraham astray, turned it into "when the nations went astray after idols, God brought me near to his fear." Abraham asks Sarah for chesed, "kindness" or loyal love, the word Ruth's story makes famous.

a: Let it be a covering of the eyes for you
p: The meaning of Abimelech's words to Sarah is uncertain. Most take the silver as public proof that she was not wronged.
b: A "covering of the eyes" probably means a payment that "covers" the matter in the eyes of others: compensation that shows publicly that Sarah has been treated honorably and that no shame attaches to her. Others think it means "so that people will look away" from her. The last words, venokhachat, "and you are set right," may mean she is vindicated before all. A thousand pieces of silver was an enormous sum: Abraham pays 400 for a burial field (23:15), and Joseph is sold for 20 (37:28). Abimelech pointedly calls Abraham "your brother."

a: Then Abraham prayed to God, and God healed Abimelech
p: The rabbis noticed that right after Abraham prays for Abimelech's household to have children, Sarah conceives.
b: The next verse is "The LORD took note of Sarah" (21:1). The Talmud draws a teaching from the order: "Whoever asks for mercy for another when he needs the same thing himself is answered first" (Bava Kamma 92a), and Rashi cites it on this verse. The verse is also the first time the Bible says God "healed" anyone (rafa'); later God names himself "the LORD, your healer" (Exodus 15:26).

a: The LORD took note of Sarah
p: The verb "paqad" means God turns his attention to someone to act. It is used for Hannah and for the Exodus.
b: Paqad (KJV "visited") means to turn one's attention to someone and act on their behalf, or sometimes to punish. God "took note of" Hannah and she bore children (1 Samuel 2:21). Joseph's last words use the same verb: "God will surely come to help you, and he will bring you up from this land" (50:24–25), and the Exodus begins when the people hear that the LORD "had taken note" of them (Exodus 4:31). The repetition, "as he had said... as he had spoken," stresses that the birth is the keeping of a word, 25 years after the first promise (12:2–4).

a: God has made laughter for me. Everyone who hears will laugh with me.
p: Sarah's laughter of doubt (18:12) becomes laughter of joy. "Laugh with me" can also mean "laugh at me."
b: Tsechoq, "laughter," gives Isaac his name. Sarah's second line, yitschaq li, can mean "will laugh with me," sharing her joy, or "will laugh at me," at an old woman nursing a baby. Both may be meant. Her words in 21:7 form a short poem, the first song of a mother in the Bible, followed later by Hannah's (1 Samuel 2:1–10) and Mary's (Luke 1:46–55). Paul quotes Isaiah's call to the barren woman to sing (Isaiah 54:1) and applies it to Sarah's children by promise (Galatians 4:27).
orig: צְחֹק עָשָׂה לִי אֱלֹהִים (tsechoq 'asah li elohim)

a: Who would have told Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?
p: The Midrash says Sarah nursed the babies of doubting neighbors, to prove Isaac was really hers.
b: Sarah says "children," plural, though she has one son. The rabbis turned the plural into a story: people whispered that the old couple had adopted a foundling, so at the weaning feast Sarah nursed the babies of all the noblewomen present, and all believed (Bava Metzia 87a; Genesis Rabbah 53:9; Rashi). The plural is probably just a general expression, but the story shows how much Jewish tradition delighted in Sarah's joy.

a: on the day Isaac was weaned Abraham held a great feast
p: Children in the ancient world nursed for two or three years. Surviving infancy was a reason to celebrate.
b: Mothers in the ancient Near East usually nursed for two or three years; a mother in 2 Maccabees 7:27 says she nursed her son three years, and Hannah brought Samuel to the temple only after he was weaned (1 Samuel 1:22–24). Many children died in infancy, so weaning was a milestone and a reason for a feast. Isaac would have been about three, and Ishmael about sixteen or seventeen.

a: laughing
p: The Hebrew says only that Ishmael was "laughing" or "playing." Readers have imagined anything from play to persecution.
b: The verb metsacheq is the same "laugh" root as Isaac's name, so the line could almost be read "Isaac-ing." It can mean laughing, joking, playing, or something worse: it is used of mocking (39:14, 17), of revelry before the golden calf (Exodus 32:6) and of Isaac's love-play with Rebekah (26:8). The Septuagint and the Vulgate add "with Isaac her son" (see the variant). The KJV has "mocking," following the rabbinic and Pauline reading. The rabbis suggested idolatry, sexual misconduct or even shooting arrows at Isaac (Genesis Rabbah 53:11; Rashi). Paul says the son "born according to the flesh persecuted" the son born by the Spirit (Galatians 4:29). Many modern readers think Ishmael did nothing wrong: Sarah saw the older son "playing Isaac," acting as the heir, and feared for her son's inheritance.

a: Throw out this slave woman and her son
p: Paul quotes Sarah's words in Galatians, reading Hagar and Sarah as two covenants.
b: Paul turns this verse into an allegory (Galatians 4:21–31). Hagar the slave woman stands for the covenant of Sinai and "the present Jerusalem," which is "in slavery with her children"; Sarah the free woman stands for "the Jerusalem above," the mother of all who live by God's promise. He quotes Sarah's demand as Scripture's verdict: "Throw out the slave woman and her son" (Galatians 4:30). Paul's point concerned believers trying to live under the Law, but the allegory was later used to set Christians against Jews, a use most Christian scholars today reject. Muslim readers object strongly to the picture of Hagar and Ishmael as the excluded line.

a: The son of this slave woman will not share the inheritance with my son
p: In ancient law, a slave woman's son might inherit if his father recognized him. Sarah moves to prevent it.
b: The Laws of Hammurabi (sections 170–171) say that if a man acknowledges the children of his slave woman as his own, they share the inheritance with his wife's children; if he does not, the slave woman and her children are set free. Ishmael, Abraham's acknowledged firstborn (16:15), had a claim. Sarah does not call Hagar by name but "this slave woman" ('amah, not the shifchah of chapter 16; scholars disagree which word is lower, and Jepsen argued that the 'amah was the one who could be a man's concubine). Deuteronomy 21:15–17 later protects the firstborn son of a less-loved wife. The narrator lets us feel Abraham's pain: "This troubled Abraham deeply, because it concerned his son" (21:11; literally "the matter was very bad in Abraham's eyes").

a: it is through Isaac that offspring will be named for you
p: Paul and Hebrews both quote this line: the promised family is defined by God's choice, not by birth alone.
b: God tells Abraham, for the second time, to listen to Sarah's voice (compare 16:2), and promises that Abraham's "offspring" in the covenant sense will be "named," or "called," through Isaac. Paul quotes it to argue that "not all who are descended from Israel are Israel," since God's promise, not physical descent alone, defines the family (Romans 9:6–8). Hebrews quotes it at the binding of Isaac: Abraham was ready to offer the very son through whom the promise was to come (Hebrews 11:17–18).

a: putting them on her shoulder, along with the boy
p: By the earlier chapters Ishmael was about sixteen, but this scene pictures a small child.
b: According to 16:16, 17:25 and 21:5–8, Ishmael would be about sixteen or seventeen. Yet the Hebrew can be read as Abraham putting the boy on Hagar's shoulder, and she later "casts" him under a bush (21:15) and lifts him up (21:18). The Septuagint says it outright: "he put the child on her shoulder." Some translations rearrange the words so that only the food and water go on her shoulder. Rashi explained that Ishmael was ill with fever, so he had to be carried. Critical scholars think the ages come from the Priestly source and this story from an older one in which Ishmael was still a child. The word yeled, "child," can be used of a young man (compare 4:23; 1 Kings 12:8).

a: I cannot watch the boy die
p: Hagar's desperate scene matches the next chapter's: a parent, a son, a journey, and an angel calling from heaven.
b: The two stories are built alike. In both, Abraham "got up early in the morning" (21:14; 22:3), a son's life is at stake in the wilderness, "the angel of God" or "of the LORD" calls "from the sky" at the last moment (21:17; 22:11), the parent's eyes are opened to see something (a well, 21:19; a ram, 22:13), and the son is promised a great future. Many readers think the narrator wants us to read Ishmael's story and Isaac's together: Abraham loses both sons, and God gives both back.

a: God has heard the boy's voice where he is
p: God hears Ishmael "where he is." The rabbis took it as judgment by what a person is now. Jews read it at the New Year.
b: The angel's words play on Ishmael's name: "God has heard." The phrase "where he is" (ba'asher hu sham) drew a famous comment. The rabbis said the angels objected: Ishmael's descendants would one day let Israel die of thirst; should God save him? God answered that he judges a person as he is at this moment (Rosh Hashanah 16b; Genesis Rabbah 53:14; Rashi). Genesis 21 is the Torah reading on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the Jewish New Year, and Genesis 22 on the second day, so Jews hear the stories of Ishmael and Isaac side by side on the day of judgment.

a: God opened her eyes, and she caught sight of a well
p: God opens Hagar's eyes to water she could not see. Muslims tell this story at Mecca, as the spring of Zamzam.
b: The well may have been there all along; what changes is Hagar's sight. In the Islamic telling (al-Bukhari), Hagar runs seven times between Safa and Marwa, an angel (in some reports, Gabriel) strikes the ground, and the spring of Zamzam bursts out in the valley of Mecca. Pilgrims drink its water to this day. The Genesis version places the scene in the wilderness of Beersheba, in the Negev. Christian writers have read God opening Hagar's eyes as a picture of grace that reveals what was hidden (compare 2 Kings 6:17; Luke 24:31).

a: He lived in the desert of Paran
p: Paran is the northern Sinai. Muslim tradition locates "Faran" in Arabia, near Mecca.
b: In the Bible the wilderness of Paran is the high desert of the northeastern Sinai, south of Kadesh, where Israel later wandered (Numbers 10:12; 13:3). Ishmael lives as a desert archer, and his Egyptian mother finds him an Egyptian wife, keeping him outside Abraham's clan. His sons' names, such as Nebaioth, Kedar and Tema (25:13–15), match Arab tribes and oases known from Assyrian records of the 700s BC onward. Muslim tradition identifies Paran (Arabic Faran) with the mountains around Mecca and reads the blessing of Ishmael as fulfilled in the Arab nation and the Prophet Muhammad.

a: Deal with me and with the land where you are living as a foreigner with the same loyalty I have dealt to you
p: Abimelech asks Abraham for "chesed," loyal kindness, the bond of a treaty between equals.
b: Chesed (see 20:13) is loyal kindness, the faithfulness people owe each other within a covenant. Here it describes a treaty between neighbors. Abimelech, who has seen that "God is with you," wants a guarantee "for my children and my descendants," a sign of how powerful Abraham has become. The same request and treaty are repeated with Isaac (26:26–31).

a: That is why the place was called Beersheba
t: "Well of the Seven" or "Well of the Oath"
p: Beersheba means "well of seven" and also "well of the oath." The seven lambs and the oath both explain it.
b: Be'er is "well," and sheva' can mean "seven" or "oath," because swearing was linked to the number seven (the verb "swear," nishba', comes from the same root). The seven lambs are the witness of the oath. Isaac later gives the name again after a new treaty (26:33). Beersheba became the southern limit of Israel ("from Dan to Beersheba," Judges 20:1). Tel Beersheba, east of the modern city, was excavated by Yohanan Aharoni; its walled town dates from the time of Israel's kings, and no Middle Bronze city has been found there, which fits Genesis, where Beersheba is a place of wells, not a town.

a: the land of the Philistines
p: The Philistines reached Canaan's coast about 1175 BC. Their mention here is one of Genesis's most debated details.
b: Egyptian records describe the "Sea Peoples," including the Peleset, attacking Egypt in the reign of Ramesses III (about 1175 BC), and archaeology shows Aegean-style pottery and culture appearing in the cities of Philistia soon after. On most chronologies that is centuries after Abraham. Critical scholars see the mention as clear evidence that the stories were written in Israel's monarchy or later, when the Philistines were familiar neighbors. Traditional scholars offer two answers: a later scribe updated the name for readers, as with "Dan" in 14:14; or earlier Aegean traders lived in the region, whom Genesis calls by the later name (the Bible links the Philistines with Caphtor, Crete, Amos 9:7). Notably, Abimelech's Philistines here are peaceful treaty partners, quite unlike those of Judges and Samuel.

a: Abraham planted a tamarisk tree
p: The tamarisk is a hardy desert tree. The Talmud said "eshel" was really an inn for travelers.
b: The tamarisk (eshel) grows in dry, salty ground and lives a long time; Saul later holds court under one (1 Samuel 22:6). Planting a tree is an act of someone who expects to stay. The Talmud records a debate: one rabbi said it was an orchard, another an inn, and later teachers read eshel as the initials of the three things Abraham gave travelers: eating (akhilah), drinking (shetiyah) and lodging (linah) (Sotah 10a; Rashi). Abraham called there on "the LORD, the Everlasting God" (El 'Olam), a title like those of other ancient gods but used here for the God who is beyond time (Isaiah 40:28).

a: God put Abraham to the test
p: The narrator tells the reader at once that this is a test. Jewish and Christian writers asked who prompted it and why.
b: The verb nissah, "test, prove," is used of God testing Israel in the wilderness "to know what was in your heart" (Deuteronomy 8:2; Exodus 20:20). The reader knows it is a test; Abraham does not. Later writers filled in the background. The book of Jubilees (about 150 BC) says the evil angel Mastema challenged God, as Satan does in Job (Jubilees 17:15–18). The Talmud says Satan accused Abraham of offering nothing at Isaac's feast (Sanhedrin 89b). James insists that God tests but "tempts no one" to evil (James 1:13). Hebrews says simply, "By faith Abraham, when he was put to the test, offered Isaac" (Hebrews 11:17). The Mishnah counts this as the last and hardest of Abraham's ten trials (Avot 5:3).

a: Here I am
p: "Here I am" is the answer of a servant ready to listen. Abraham says it three times in this chapter.
b: Hinneni, "here I am," is more than a statement of place; it means "I am ready, I am listening." Abraham says it to God (22:1), to his son (22:7) and to the angel (22:11), the three voices that pull at him in the story. Moses says it at the burning bush (Exodus 3:4), Samuel in the night (1 Samuel 3:4) and Isaiah in the temple (Isaiah 6:8). On the High Holy Days the cantor's personal prayer before the additional service begins with the same word.

a: your son, please, your only one, whom you love, Isaac
p: God names Isaac in four steps, each closer. Abraham had two sons; why "only"? The Greek says "beloved."
b: The command tightens like a knot: "your son, please, your only one, whom you love, Isaac." Rashi, following the Midrash, imagined a dialogue: "I have two sons." "Your only one." "Each is the only one of his mother." "Whom you love." "I love them both." "Isaac" (Sanhedrin 89b; Genesis Rabbah 55:7). Yachid, "only one," means unique and irreplaceable; after Ishmael was sent away, Isaac was the only son left at home and the only son of the promise. The Septuagint translated it agapētos, "beloved," the word God uses at Jesus' baptism: "You are my dearly loved Son" (Mark 1:11). This is also the first time the Bible uses the word "love."
orig: אֶת־בִּנְךָ אֶת־יְחִידְךָ אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ אֶת־יִצְחָק (et-binkha et-yechidkha asher-ahavta et-yitschaq)

a: go to the land of Moriah
p: Chronicles puts Mount Moriah in Jerusalem, where the Temple was built. Samaritans and Muslims place the scene elsewhere.
b: The only other "Moriah" in the Bible is "Mount Moriah" in Jerusalem, where Solomon built the temple (2 Chronicles 3:1), and 22:14 hints at the same place ("the mountain of the LORD"). Jewish tradition holds that the rock under the Holy of Holies, the Foundation Stone, is the altar of Isaac; it lies today under the Dome of the Rock. The Samaritans read "the land of Moreh" (see the variant) and place the binding on Mount Gerizim, near Shechem. Many Muslims place the sacrifice at Mina near Mecca, where pilgrims sacrifice animals at the feast of Eid al-Adha. Beersheba to Jerusalem is about 50 miles, a three-day walk (22:4).

a: There offer him up as a burnt offering
t: A God who asks for a child?
p: Child sacrifice was practiced around Israel and forbidden by Israel's law. How then could God command it?
b: A burnt offering ('olah, "what goes up") was burned whole on the altar. Israel's neighbors sometimes sacrificed children: the king of Moab offered his firstborn son on the city wall (2 Kings 3:27), and the prophets condemn the practice in Israel itself (Jeremiah 7:31). The Law forbids it outright (Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31), and God says through Jeremiah it is something "I never commanded, and it never came into my mind" (Jeremiah 19:5). Readers answer in several ways. Many Jewish and Christian readers say God never intended the death; the test was of Abraham's trust, and its ending forever rejected child sacrifice. Some critical scholars see the story as an older tale reshaped to replace child sacrifice with animal sacrifice. Jon Levenson argues that Israel kept the idea that the firstborn belongs to God, transformed into redemption (Exodus 13:13). Immanuel Kant answered that Abraham should have replied that a voice ordering him to kill his innocent son could not be God's (The Conflict of the Faculties, 1798); others, from Kierkegaard to modern ethicists, insist the command remains deeply disturbing.
r: 2 Kings 3:27; Leviticus 18:21; Deuteronomy 12:31; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5; Judges 11:30–40; Exodus 13:13; Micah 6:7

a: Abraham got up early in the morning
p: Abraham argued for Sodom but says nothing for his son. Readers from the rabbis to Kierkegaard have wondered why.
b: The verbs pile up without a word of feeling: got up, saddled, took, split, set out. Abraham who argued with God for strangers in Sodom (18:23–32) does not argue for his own son. Rashi notes that a man of his wealth saddled his own donkey: love made him eager to obey. Erich Auerbach, in a famous essay, contrasted this spare, silent telling, "fraught with background," with Homer's full descriptions. The Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard (Fear and Trembling, 1843) retold the scene four times to show how unthinkable Abraham's faith is: a "knight of faith" who trusts God beyond the limits of ethics. Some modern readers think Abraham failed, or was meant to refuse: Lippman Bodoff (1993) argued that the real test was whether he would stop short, and Omri Boehm (2007) that the angel scene was added to an older story in which Abraham chose not to kill. Most tradition says he passed.

a: On the third day
p: The third day is a turning point in many Bible stories. Christians connect it to the resurrection.
b: Three days of walking gave Abraham time to turn back. The third day is a day of crisis and deliverance across the Bible: Joseph's brothers are released on the third day (42:18), God comes down on Sinai on the third day (Exodus 19:11, 16), Esther goes to the king on the third day (Esther 5:1), and Hosea promises, "on the third day he will raise us up" (Hosea 6:2). Christian writers saw a foreshadowing of Jesus raised on the third day. The rabbis noticed the same pattern (Genesis Rabbah 56:1).
r: 42:18; Exodus 19:11; Hosea 6:2; Jonah 1:17; Esther 5:1; Matthew 16:21; 1 Corinthians 15:4

a: We will worship, and then we will come back to you
p: Abraham says "we." Hebrews reads it as faith that God could raise Isaac from the dead.
b: The verbs are plural: "we will worship, we will come back." Was Abraham hiding the truth from the servants, hoping, or believing? Hebrews answers: "He reasoned that God could even raise the dead, and in a manner of speaking he did receive Isaac back from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). Rashi says Abraham prophesied without knowing it. Paul calls God the one "who gives life to the dead and calls into being things that do not exist" when speaking of Abraham's faith (Romans 4:17).

a: laid it on his son Isaac
p: Isaac carries the wood up the mountain. The Midrash compared him to a man carrying his own cross.
b: The son carries the wood for his own sacrifice; the father carries the fire and the knife. The Midrash says Isaac carried the wood "like one who carries his cross on his shoulder" (Genesis Rabbah 56:3), a striking phrase from a Jewish source of the 400s AD, probably reflecting Roman crucifixion. Early Christian writers, such as Melito of Sardis (about AD 170) and Tertullian, saw Isaac carrying the wood as a picture of Jesus "carrying his own cross" (John 19:17). Isaac, old enough to carry a load of wood uphill, was no small child.

a: And the two of them walked on together
p: The line is repeated before and after Isaac's question. They walk "as one."
b: Vayyelkhu shenehem yachdav, "the two of them walked together," appears twice (22:6, 8), framing the only conversation between father and son in the Bible. Rashi said that the first time Abraham knew and Isaac did not; the second time, after "God will see to the lamb... my son," both knew, and they still walked together "with one heart." The word yachdav also returns at the end, when Abraham and the young men go "together" to Beersheba (22:19), but Isaac is not named.

a: God will see to the lamb for a burnt offering himself, my son
p: The verb is "see": God will see to it, provide it. A midrash reads the words as "the lamb... is you, my son."
b: "Will see to" is yir'eh, "will see." To "see to" something is to provide it, as in English. The word returns in the name Abraham gives the place, "The LORD Will See" (22:14), and links to Hagar's "God who sees" (16:13). The sentence can be read two ways: "God will provide the lamb, my son," or, with a pause, "God will provide the lamb: my son." A midrash takes it the second way: Isaac understood that he was the lamb and went on willingly. Christians hear John the Baptist's words, "There is the Lamb of God" (John 1:29), and Revelation's Lamb (Revelation 5:6).

a: He bound his son Isaac
t: The Akedah: how old was Isaac?
p: "Bound" gives the story its Jewish name, the Akedah. Jewish tradition made Isaac a grown man who consented.
b: The verb 'aqad, "bind," appears only here in the Bible, and the story is called in Hebrew 'Aqedat Yitschaq, "the Binding of Isaac." The text gives no age. Josephus says Isaac was twenty-five and ran gladly to the altar (Antiquities 1.227–232). The Midrash, reasoning that Sarah died at 127 right after (23:1), made him thirty-seven (Genesis Rabbah). The Targums have Isaac ask his father to bind him tightly so he would not flinch and spoil the offering. In these readings Isaac is a willing martyr, a model for Jews who died for their faith; medieval Jewish poems written after massacres in the Crusades recalled the Akedah. Christians read the willing son as a picture of Christ (Philippians 2:8).

a: Abraham! Abraham!
p: A doubled name marks an urgent call from God, as with Jacob, Moses and Samuel.
b: God calls twice by name at turning points: "Jacob, Jacob" (46:2), "Moses, Moses" (Exodus 3:4), "Samuel, Samuel" (1 Samuel 3:10), and in the New Testament "Martha, Martha" (Luke 10:41) and "Saul, Saul" (Acts 9:4). The rabbis said the doubling shows love and urgency. The angel of the LORD speaks here, as to Hagar in the previous chapter, "from the sky" (21:17).

a: Now I know that you fear God
p: If God knows all things, how can he say "now I know"? Jewish and Christian commentators answered in different ways.
b: Rashi read it as "now I can show the world" (and answer Satan and the nations) "that you fear me." Ramban explained that a test makes actual what was only possible: God knew Abraham's heart, but the deed gave Abraham the reward of having done it. Many Christian theologians say God speaks in human terms. Some modern theologians, such as those who hold "open theism," take the words more literally. All agree on the result: "you fear God," the very quality Abraham doubted in Gerar (20:11). Abraham is the only person in Genesis said to "fear God" by God himself.

a: in place of his son
p: The ram dies "in place of" Isaac. Christians, Jews and Muslims each see in it a key to their faith.
b: Tachat beno, "instead of his son," is the first clear substitution in the Bible. For Christians it pictures atonement: God "did not hold back his own Son. He handed him over for us all" (Romans 8:32), the son of Abraham whom no ram replaced. For Jews the ram's horn, the shofar, blown on the New Year, recalls the binding: "Blow before me a ram's horn, so that I may remember for you the binding of Isaac" (Rosh Hashanah 16a), and daily prayers ask God to remember the Akedah. The Qur'an tells the story with an unnamed son who agrees ("Father, do as you are commanded"), and says "We ransomed him with a great sacrifice" (Qur'an 37:102–107). Muslims remember it every year at Eid al-Adha, the Feast of Sacrifice. Early Muslim scholars debated whether the son was Isaac or Ishmael; most later scholars, such as Ibn Kathir, held it was Ishmael.
orig: תַּחַת בְּנוֹ (tachat beno), "in place of his son"

a: "The LORD Will See."
t: "The LORD will provide" or "will be seen"?
p: The name plays on "see": the LORD sees (provides), and on his mountain he is seen. The Temple mount is in view.
b: YHWH yir'eh means "the LORD will see," that is, see to it, provide (compare 22:8; KJV "Jehovah-jireh"). The saying that follows uses the passive, yera'eh, "on the mountain of the LORD he will be seen" or "it will be provided." Pilgrims "appeared" before the LORD at the temple three times a year (Exodus 23:17), using the same verb, and "the mountain of the LORD" is a regular name for Zion (Isaiah 2:3; Psalm 24:3). The Midrash even explained the name Jerusalem as Yir'eh (Abraham's name for it) joined to Shalem (Melchizedek's, 14:18) (Genesis Rabbah 56:10).
orig: יְהוָה יִרְאֶה... בְּהַר יְהוָה יֵרָאֶה (YHWH yir'eh... behar YHWH yera'eh)

a: By myself I swear, says the LORD
p: God swears by himself, the only oath he speaks aloud in Abraham's story. Hebrews: there was no one greater to swear by.
b: God's promises to Abraham become an oath. Later Scripture remembers it as "the oath that he swore to Abraham" (26:3; Luke 1:73), and Joseph dies trusting "the land he swore to give Abraham, Isaac and Jacob" (50:24). Hebrews explains: "because there was no one greater for him to swear by, he swore by himself," so that "by two things that cannot change," his promise and his oath, believers might have hope as "an anchor for our lives" (Hebrews 6:13–19). "Says the LORD" (ne'um YHWH, often "declares the LORD"), common in the prophets, appears only here in Genesis.

a: Your offspring will take over the gate of his enemies
p: To hold a city's gate was to hold the city. Rebekah's family blesses her with the same words.
b: The gate was the strong point of a city and the seat of its government (19:1), so to "possess the gate" meant to conquer. Rebekah's family gives her the same blessing when she leaves to marry Isaac: "may your offspring take over the gate of those who hate him" (24:60). Jesus may echo the image when he says "the gates of Hades will not overcome" his church (Matthew 16:18). The Hebrew suffix is singular, "his enemies," because "offspring" is a collective singular; the Plain English keeps it, since Paul builds on the singular "offspring" (Galatians 3:16) and later Jewish and Christian readers heard a single heir in it. On the stars and the sand, see 13:16.
orig: וְיִרַשׁ זַרְעֲךָ אֵת שַׁעַר אֹיְבָיו (veyirash zar'akha et sha'ar oyevav)

a: because you have listened to my voice
p: The promise of 12:3 returns, now tied to Abraham's obedience. Peter quotes this form of it in Acts.
b: The blessing of 12:3 is repeated with two changes: "your offspring" instead of "you," and a clearly reflexive verb (hitbarekhu; see 12:3). And it is now linked to obedience: "because you have listened to my voice," as later "because Abraham listened to my voice and kept what I required of him" (26:5). Peter quotes it to the crowd in the temple: "In your offspring all the families of the earth will be blessed," and applies it to Jesus (Acts 3:25–26). Paul builds on the singular "offspring" (Galatians 3:16).

a: Then Abraham went back to his servants
p: Isaac is not mentioned coming down the mountain. Some later traditions imagined that he died, or went away to study.
b: Abraham returns "to his servants" (literally "his young men"), and they go "together" to Beersheba, but Isaac is not named; he next appears coming from Beer-lahai-roi (24:62). Most readers assume he came back too, unmentioned. But the silence fed legends. One Midrash says Abraham sent him to study at the school of Shem (Genesis Rabbah 56:11). Some medieval Jewish sources even told that Isaac was actually slain and his ashes lay on the altar, then he was revived; Shalom Spiegel traced these traditions in The Last Trial (1950, English 1967). Abraham ibn Ezra rejected such readings as contrary to the text. Some critical scholars suggest that an older (Elohist) version of the story ended differently, since only Abraham is said to return. Sarah, too, is not mentioned, and in the next chapter she dies at Hebron.

a: Milcah too has borne children to your brother Nahor
t: Nahor's twelve sons and the introduction of Rebekah
p: Nahor has twelve sons, like Ishmael and Jacob. The list's real purpose is its last line: Rebekah.
b: Nahor's eight sons by his wife and four by his concubine make twelve, matching the twelve sons of Ishmael (25:13–16) and of Jacob (35:22–26). Several names are those of Aramean and Arabian peoples: Uz is Job's homeland (Job 1:1), Elihu was a Buzite (Job 32:2), and Aram is Syria; Chesed recalls the Chaldeans (kasdim). Maacah became an Aramean kingdom north of Israel (2 Samuel 10:6). Right after the promise of offspring, the narrator quietly introduces Rebekah, granddaughter of Abraham's brother, who will be Isaac's wife (24:15).

a: The life of Sarah came to a hundred and twenty-seven years
p: Sarah is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is given. The rabbis linked her death to the binding of Isaac.
b: Genesis gives the lifespans of the ancestors, but for no other woman. The odd wording, literally "a hundred years and twenty years and seven years," led Rashi to say each part has its own praise: at a hundred she was as free of sin as at twenty, and at twenty as beautiful as at seven. Because her death follows straight after chapter 22, the Midrash and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan say she died of shock when she heard that Abraham had taken Isaac to be sacrificed (Genesis Rabbah 58:5; Rashi on 23:2). The rabbis also noted that Queen Esther, her descendant, ruled 127 provinces (Esther 1:1; Genesis Rabbah 58:3). Isaiah calls Israel to "look at Sarah who gave you birth" (Isaiah 51:2), 1 Peter praises her character, and Hebrews 11:11 her faith (though many read that verse as being about Abraham).

a: Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron
p: Kiriath-arba means "town of four" or "town of Arba." Jewish tradition counted four couples buried there.
b: Joshua explains the old name: Arba was "the greatest man among the Anakim," the giant clan of the region (Joshua 14:15; 15:13). The rabbis read "four" and said it was the burial place of four couples: Adam and Eve, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Leah (Rashi). In the Masoretic Text, the word "and to weep for her" is written with a small kaf, one of several small letters in the Torah; one later explanation is that Abraham wept only a little, since Sarah died at a full old age. Abraham "came" to mourn, perhaps from Beersheba (22:19).

a: the sons of Heth
p: The great Hittite empire was in Turkey. Genesis's "sons of Heth" live in Hebron. Who were they?
b: Genesis traces Heth to Canaan (10:15), so the "sons of Heth" are presented as one of the peoples of the land (15:20). The famous Hittite empire ruled central Anatolia (modern Turkey) from about 1650 to 1180 BC, far from Hebron. After it fell, smaller "Neo-Hittite" kingdoms survived in Syria, and Assyrian records of the 800s–700s BC used "Hatti" loosely for all of Syria and Canaan. Many critical scholars therefore see the Hittites of Hebron as a later writer's label. Conservative scholars such as Kitchen suggest a small group with names like Heth who were unrelated to the Anatolian empire, or migrants from it; the names Ephron and Zohar are Semitic, not Hittite. The question remains open.

a: I am a foreigner living among you as a settler
p: Abraham owns nothing in the promised land. His words become a confession of the whole people of God.
b: Ger vetoshav, "a foreigner and a settler," describes someone who lives among a people without belonging. Sixty-two years after God promised him the land, Abraham does not own a grave. God later tells Israel, "the land is mine. You are foreigners and lodgers living with me" (Leviticus 25:23). David prays, "We are foreigners before you, and settlers, as all our fathers were" (1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 39:12). Hebrews says the ancestors "admitted that they were foreigners and temporary residents on the earth," looking for a better country (Hebrews 11:13–16), and 1 Peter calls Christians "foreigners and temporary residents" (1 Peter 2:11).
r: Leviticus 25:23; 1 Chronicles 29:15; Psalm 39:12; Hebrews 11:9–16; 1 Peter 2:11; Acts 7:5

a: You are a prince of God among us
p: The Hebrew is "a prince of God." It may mean "a mighty prince," or that the locals see God's hand on Abraham.
b: Nesi' elohim can be taken literally, "a prince of God," a leader marked by divine favor (compare 21:22, "God is with you in all you do"), or as a Hebrew way of saying "very great," as "mountains of God" means mighty mountains (Psalm 36:6). Abraham calls himself a landless foreigner; the people of Hebron call him a prince. The difference sets the tone for the polite bargaining that follows.

a: at its full price in silver
p: Abraham insists on paying in full before witnesses at the town gate, so no one can ever take the land back.
b: The whole scene is a legal transaction. It happens at the gate, where the town's men gathered (23:10, 18; Ruth 4:1–11), in their "hearing" and "before their eyes," the phrases of witnessed contracts. Abraham asks for "full silver" (kesef male'), the same phrase David uses when he insists on paying for the threshing floor that became the temple site (1 Chronicles 21:22–24). A gift could be taken back; a purchase could not. In 1953 Manfred Lehmann argued that Hittite laws explained why Ephron insisted on selling the whole field, so that feudal duties would pass to Abraham. Later scholars, notably Gene Tucker (1966), showed that the closest parallels are first-millennium BC "dialogue contracts" from Babylonia, a point some use for dating.

a: Land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between you and me?
p: Ephron names a high price while pretending it is nothing. The rabbis saw a man who said much and did little.
b: After offering the field "free" three times (23:11), Ephron mentions its value in passing, and the price is steep. Four hundred shekels is about 10 pounds of silver. Jeremiah later buys a field for 17 shekels (Jeremiah 32:9), David pays 50 for the threshing floor (2 Samuel 24:24), and Omri pays two talents (6,000 shekels) for the whole hill of Samaria (1 Kings 16:24). Abraham pays without a word. The rabbis noticed that in 23:16 Ephron's name is spelled without the letter vav, and said it was shortened because "he said much but did not do even a little" (Bava Metzia 87a; Rashi). Many readers see an ordinary bargaining courtesy, still known in Middle Eastern markets.

a: at the merchants' standard weight
p: There were no coins yet. Silver was weighed on scales, by weights accepted among traders.
b: Coins were first made in Lydia (western Turkey) around 600 BC. Before that, payment was made by weighing silver, often in broken pieces and rings (archaeologists call it "hacksilver"), on balance scales with stone or metal weights. A "shekel" was a weight, roughly 11 to 12 grams. "Current among merchants" means silver of the standard weight and quality that traders would accept. The Law later demanded honest weights (Leviticus 19:35–36), and the prophets condemned merchants who cheated with false scales (Amos 8:5).

a: the cave of the field of Machpelah facing Mamre
p: The traditional tomb stands in Hebron inside walls built by Herod. Jews, Christians and Muslims all revere it.
b: Abraham (25:9), Isaac, Rebekah, Leah and Jacob (49:29–32; 50:13) were later buried here. The traditional site in Hebron is enclosed by massive stone walls built in the time of Herod the Great (late first century BC), still standing to their full height. It is known in Hebrew as Me'arat ha-Makhpelah and in Arabic as the Ibrahimi Mosque (al-Haram al-Ibrahimi). It has been a Byzantine church, a mosque, a Crusader church and a mosque again, and today it is divided into Jewish and Muslim sections. The caves beneath have been entered only rarely and have never been excavated. "Machpelah" may mean "double," and the rabbis said it was a cave with two levels or for couples.

a: So the field and the cave in it passed from the sons of Heth to Abraham
t: The first piece of the promise
p: Abraham's only land in Canaan is a grave. Stephen later says he owned "not even a foot" of it.
b: God promised Abraham all the land (13:15; 15:18), but the only part he ever owns is a burial cave, bought at full price. The narrator repeats the legal formula twice (23:17, 20), as if to stress that this small piece, at least, is legally Abraham's forever. Stephen says God gave Abraham "no share of it to inherit, not even room to plant a foot" (Acts 7:5); he also speaks of a tomb Abraham bought at Shechem (Acts 7:16), apparently blending this purchase with Jacob's at Shechem (33:19; Joshua 24:32). Many readers see the grave as a pledge: the dead are buried in the land of promise in hope of the rest.

a: Abraham said to his servant, the oldest of his household
p: The servant is never named. Jewish tradition calls him Eliezer; Christian preachers saw a picture of the Holy Spirit.
b: The longest chapter in Genesis is carried by a man whose name it never gives. Jewish tradition identifies him with Eliezer of Damascus (15:2) and praises his faithfulness (Genesis Rabbah 59–60; Rashi). The rabbis noted that the chapter tells his story twice in full, and said "the ordinary talk of the patriarchs' servants is dearer to God than the Torah of their children" (Genesis Rabbah 60:8). Many Christian preachers, especially in the Reformed and evangelical traditions, read the chapter as an allegory: the father (Abraham) sends his servant (the Holy Spirit) to a far country to bring a bride (the church) for his son (Christ), who waits to meet her. The text itself simply presents a model of loyal, prayerful service.

a: Put your hand under my thigh
p: The "thigh" is probably a polite word for the genitals. The oath touches the source of Abraham's descendants.
b: The same gesture appears only once more, when Jacob makes Joseph swear to bury him in Canaan (47:29). "Thigh" (yarekh) can stand for the reproductive organs, as descendants are said to come "from the thigh" of Jacob (46:26; Exodus 1:5). An oath sworn this way touched the source of life and family, and perhaps the sign of the covenant: Rashi says the servant swore on the circumcision. Both oaths concern the future of Abraham's line and its tie to the land. Elsewhere in the ancient world, oaths were sworn while touching sacred objects.
orig: שִׂים־נָא יָדְךָ תַּחַת יְרֵכִי (sim-na yadkha tachat yerekhi)

a: that you will not take a wife for my son from the daughters of the Canaanites
p: Abraham insists Isaac not marry a Canaanite. Later law and the books of Ezra and Nehemiah take up the same concern.
b: Marrying within one's clan was normal in the ancient world. Here it also has a religious point: the covenant line must not be absorbed into the peoples of the land. Esau's Hittite wives grieve Isaac and Rebekah (26:34–35), and Jacob is sent to the same family to find a wife (27:46–28:2). The Law later forbids Israel to intermarry with the Canaanites "for they will turn your sons away from following me" (Deuteronomy 7:3–4), and Ezra and Nehemiah enforce this after the exile (Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:23–27). Yet Genesis also records Joseph marrying an Egyptian (41:45) and Judah a Canaanite (38:2), and Ruth shows a foreign woman joining Israel. Christian teaching applied the principle to marriage between believers (2 Corinthians 6:14).

a: he will send his angel ahead of you
t: An angel to guide the way
p: Abraham trusts that God's angel will go ahead. The promise returns to Israel at Sinai, and in the book of Tobit.
b: Abraham, who received the promise, speaks his last recorded words here, and they are a confession of trust. God makes the same promise to Israel: "I am sending an angel before you to keep you safe on the road" (Exodus 23:20; 33:2). The Jewish book of Tobit, from about 200 BC, tells a story clearly modeled on this chapter: a young man travels east to find a wife from his own kin, guided by the angel Raphael in disguise. Psalm 91:11 promises angels to guard the faithful "in all your ways."

a: Aram-naharaim, to the town of Nahor
p: "Aram-naharaim" means "Aram of the two rivers," upper Mesopotamia. A town called Nahur is known from ancient letters.
b: Aram-naharaim (Greek "Mesopotamia," "between the rivers") is the land between the upper Euphrates and the Habur and Balikh rivers, around Haran (27:43; 28:10). "The town of Nahor" may mean the town where Nahor lived, perhaps Haran itself, or a real town: letters from Mari (1700s BC) mention a town Nahur in that region, and Assyrian texts know a Til-Nakhiri, "mound of Nahor," near Haran. The trip from Hebron or Beersheba is over 500 miles, a journey of several weeks by camel. On the camels themselves, see 12:16.

a: by the well outside the town
p: Three of the Bible's great love stories begin at a well. Jesus meets a Samaritan woman at one too.
b: Robert Alter calls this a "type scene": a man travels to a foreign land, meets a young woman at a well, water is drawn, she runs home to tell her family, and a marriage follows. It happens here, with Jacob and Rachel (29:1–14), and with Moses and Zipporah (Exodus 2:15–21). Each version is told differently to show character: here the servant prays and Rebekah does all the work; Jacob rolls the stone himself; Moses defends the women. Many readers see John 4 as a deliberate echo, with Jesus at Jacob's well speaking with a Samaritan woman about "living water."

a: let it happen for me today
p: The servant asks God for a sign to identify the bride. The Talmud thought he asked carelessly.
b: "Let it happen" (haqreh) uses the verb for chance events: the servant asks God to direct what looks like chance (compare Ruth 2:3). He sets a test: the right woman will offer water not only to him but also to his camels, a sign of generosity and hard work. The Talmud lists him among three who "asked improperly," since an unsuitable woman might have passed the test; God answered him well anyway (Taanit 4a). Gideon's fleece is another such request (Judges 6:36–40). Many Christian writers caution against demanding signs, while praising the servant's habit of prayer at every step (24:26–27, 52).

a: a virgin whom no man had been with
t: Two words for a young woman
p: Here Rebekah is a "betulah"; in 24:43 the servant calls her an "almah." The pair matters for Isaiah 7:14.
b: The narrator calls Rebekah na'arah ("young woman"), betulah ("virgin," or a young woman of marriageable age) and adds "no man had known her" to make the point plain. In retelling, the servant calls her an 'almah (24:43), "young woman," the word in Isaiah's sign: "the 'almah will conceive and bear a son" (Isaiah 7:14). Since Rebekah is both a betulah and an 'almah, Christians have pointed to this chapter to argue that 'almah can describe a virgin, as the Septuagint rendered it in Isaiah (parthenos) and Matthew quotes it (Matthew 1:23). Jewish interpreters reply that 'almah itself means only "young woman." Both readings appeal to this chapter.
r: 24:43; Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23; Exodus 2:8; Song of Songs 6:8

a: drew water for all his camels
p: A thirsty camel can drink over 25 gallons. Rebekah's offer meant dozens of trips with a jar.
b: A camel that has gone without water on a long trip can drink 25 to 30 gallons or more. Ten camels might need well over a hundred gallons, drawn jar by jar from a spring "down" a slope (24:16) and carried back to the trough. The narrator piles up her verbs: she hurried, emptied, ran, drew. Rebekah's generosity goes far beyond what the servant's test required, and shows the energy and decisiveness she will show again (25:22–23; 27:5–17).

a: a gold ring weighing a beka, half a shekel
p: The KJV says "earring" and that the servant put it "upon her face." The Hebrew means a nose ring.
b: A nezem can be worn in the ear (35:4) or the nose, and 24:47 makes it clear: "I put the ring on her nose" ('al-appah). The KJV, perhaps uneasy with the custom, wrote "earring" and "upon her face." Nose rings were common jewelry in the ancient Near East (Isaiah 3:21; Ezekiel 16:12). The weights are a "beka," half a shekel, about a fifth of an ounce, and ten shekels, about four ounces of gold for the bracelets: a lavish gift that announced the wealth of the suitor's family.
orig: נֶזֶם זָהָב בֶּקַע מִשְׁקָלוֹ (nezem zahav beqa' mishqalo)

a: his loyal love and faithfulness
p: "Loyal love and faithfulness" is one of the Bible's great word pairs, used of God in Exodus 34:6.
b: Chesed ve'emet joins loyal, covenant love with reliability, truth. God describes himself as "great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6), rav chesed ve'emet, and the pair runs through the Psalms (Psalm 25:10; 85:10). John's Gospel may echo it: the Word was "full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). The servant uses the pair twice, of God (24:27) and in asking Rebekah's family to act the same way (24:49). In this chapter God's faithfulness is shown not through a miracle but through the ordinary steps of a journey: "the LORD has led me on the road."

a: As soon as he had seen the ring and the bracelets
p: Laban runs out only after he sees the jewelry. Readers who know chapters 29–31 smile at the hint.
b: The narrator lets Laban's welcome follow his glimpse of gold: first he sees the ring and bracelets, then he runs to "the man blessed by the LORD." Rashi comments, "He saw the ring and said, this man is rich," and the Midrash paints Laban as greedy from the start. Readers who know how Laban later tricks Jacob and changes his wages ten times (29:21–27; 31:7) will see the warning. Others think this is too harsh: Laban's hospitality is real and his words pious (24:31, 50).

a: I will not eat until I have told my errand
p: The servant puts his master's errand before his own hunger, a picture Jesus echoes.
b: After a journey of weeks, the servant refuses the meal until his task is explained. Jesus, sitting at a well while his disciples bring food, says, "Doing what the one who sent me wants, and bringing his work to completion: that is my food" (John 4:34). The servant's single-mindedness is the picture of what a faithful agent should be (Luke 12:42–43).

a: I am Abraham's servant
p: The servant repeats the whole story to Rebekah's family, but not word for word. His changes are revealing.
b: Ancient storytellers often repeated a scene, and listeners enjoyed noticing the differences. The servant's version (24:34–49) leaves out Abraham's insistence that Isaac must never go back east, which could insult the family. It stresses God's blessing and Isaac's inheritance (24:35–36), speaks of Abraham's "father's house" and "clan" rather than his "land," and puts the gifts after he learns her family (24:47; in 24:22 he gave them first). Robert Alter and other literary critics see a skillful diplomat at work. The rabbis saw something else: the Torah spends this many words on a servant's speech, while it gives important laws in a single verse (Genesis Rabbah 60:8).

a: This has come from the LORD
p: Rebekah's father is named here, but afterward only her brother and mother act. The Midrash explained why.
b: Laban and Bethuel answer together, but from then on it is "her brother and her mother" who speak (24:53, 55), and the household is "her mother's" (24:28). The Midrash said Bethuel tried to stop the marriage and an angel struck him dead (Rashi on 24:55); a later legend adds that he ate poisoned food meant for the servant. Many modern scholars think the name Bethuel was added here by a later hand, or that the brother naturally took the lead in arranging a sister's marriage, as with Dinah's brothers (34:11–13). Their reply, "from the LORD," shows the family recognizing God's hand.

a: She said, "I will go."
p: Rebekah's family asks her, and she says yes in one word. The rabbis drew a rule: a woman must consent to marriage.
b: In Hebrew her answer is one word, elekh, "I will go," the verb of Abraham's call, "Go" (12:1). Like Abraham, Rebekah leaves land, family and father's house for a land she has never seen. Rashi takes the family's question as the source of a rule: "From here we learn that a woman is not married off except with her consent" (Genesis Rabbah 60:12; compare Kiddushin 41a). Rebekah's quick decision fits her character: she acts with the same speed she showed at the well.

a: may your offspring take over
p: The family's farewell blessing echoes God's oath to Abraham. Jewish weddings still recite it.
b: Rebekah's family blesses her with words nearly identical to God's oath in 22:17: "Your offspring will take over the gate of his enemies." "Thousands of ten thousands" is the language of great numbers (Numbers 10:36; Deuteronomy 33:17). At a traditional Jewish wedding, before the ceremony, the groom lowers the veil over the bride's face (the bedeken), and the words "Our sister, may you become thousands of ten thousands" are said over her.

a: Now Isaac had come from the way to Beer-lahai-roi
p: Isaac is living near the well where God saw Hagar. The Midrash said he had gone to bring Hagar back for his father.
b: Beer-lahai-roi is where the angel found Hagar (16:14), and Isaac will settle there after Abraham's death (25:11). Isaac's first appearance since Mount Moriah is at the well of the God who sees. The Midrash said he had gone there to bring Hagar back to be his father's wife, identifying her with Keturah (25:1; Genesis Rabbah 60:14; Rashi). The text does not say so, but the place quietly links Abraham's two sons.

a: Isaac had gone out toward evening to muse in the field
t: What was Isaac doing in the field?
p: The verb "lasuach" is found nowhere else. Rabbis said "to pray"; others say "to walk" or "to stroll."
b: The meaning of lasuach is uncertain. The rabbis connected it with siach, "talk, complaint, prayer" (Psalm 102:1), and said Isaac instituted the afternoon prayer, Minchah, just as Abraham instituted the morning prayer (19:27) and Jacob the evening prayer (28:11) (Berakhot 26b). The Septuagint has "to meditate" or "to ponder," followed by the KJV. Some modern scholars connect it with a verb meaning "to walk about" or "to roam," and a few with other meanings. The Plain English "muse" keeps the traditional sense without deciding between prayer and quiet thought.

a: So she took her veil and covered her face
p: Rebekah veils herself when she sees her husband. Veiling seems to have marked a bride before her wedding.
b: The tsa'if was a wrap or veil. Rebekah covers herself as a bride approaching her husband, a modest gesture of a woman about to be married. Tamar later uses the same garment for a very different purpose (38:14, 19). Laban's trick on Jacob, giving him the veiled Leah instead of Rachel, may depend on the bride being veiled (29:23–25). On the Jewish custom of the groom veiling the bride, see 24:60.

a: and he loved her. So Isaac was comforted after his mother.
p: This is the first time the Bible says a husband loved his wife.
b: "He loved her" (vayye'ehaveha): only the second use of "love" in the Bible was for Abraham's love for Isaac (22:2), and now Isaac loves Rebekah, the first time a husband's love for his wife is named. Jacob will love Rachel (29:18), and Elkanah Hannah (1 Samuel 1:5). The order is notable: marriage first, then love, as in many arranged marriages. Bringing her into "the tent of Sarah his mother" makes Rebekah the new mother of the family. The rabbis said the signs of blessing in Sarah's tent returned with her (Genesis Rabbah 60:16; Rashi). Isaac, about forty (25:20), had mourned his mother for about three years.

a: her name was Keturah
p: Keturah appears only here and in 1 Chronicles. The Midrash and Rashi say she was Hagar under a new name.
b: The text does not say when Abraham married Keturah; the Hebrew "and Abraham again took a wife" may follow Sarah's death or simply add an old record. 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her Abraham's concubine, as 25:6 implies. Some rabbis identified her with Hagar, saying Isaac had fetched her back from Beer-lahai-roi (24:62) and that her name, from the word for incense, means her deeds were fragrant (Genesis Rabbah 61:4; Rashi). Ibn Ezra and Ramban took her to be a different woman, and most modern readers agree. Her six sons carry the names of peoples and places in Arabia, so the list ties Abraham to the tribes of the incense trade.

a: Midian
p: Midian, Sheba and Dedan are known peoples of northwest Arabia. The list links Israel to its desert neighbors.
b: Midian lived east of the Gulf of Aqaba; Moses married a Midianite (Exodus 2:15–21), and later Midian raided Israel (Judges 6). Dedan is the oasis of al-Ula in Saudi Arabia, named in inscriptions there and in Babylonian texts. Sheba was a kingdom of southern Arabia, also listed under Shem and Ham (10:7, 28). Critical scholars note that these peoples are best attested in the first millennium BC and see the list as reflecting the caravan trade of that age. Traditional readers see families that later grew into tribes. Either way, Genesis presents Israel's neighbors as distant kin.

a: made gifts
p: Abraham provides for the other sons but sends them east, keeping the inheritance for Isaac.
b: This repeats the pattern of Ishmael's sending away (21:14) but more gently: these sons receive gifts while Abraham is alive. The inheritance and the promise go to Isaac alone (25:5; 21:12). The Talmud says Abraham gave them "a name of impurity," that is, knowledge of occult arts, which they took to the East (Sanhedrin 91a); later Jewish writers linked this with the wisdom of India and the East. "The land of the East" (qedem) is the steppe and desert east of Canaan, home of the "people of the East" (Judges 6:3; Job 1:3).

a: he was gathered to his people
p: The phrase is not the same as burial. Many readers take it as a hint of life with one's ancestors after death.
b: Abraham is "gathered to his people" before he is buried, and far from where his ancestors lie (11:32). The phrase is used for Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, Aaron and Moses (25:17; 35:29; 49:33; Numbers 20:24; Deuteronomy 32:50), and Moses' grave was never found (Deuteronomy 34:6). So many scholars, critical and traditional, think it once meant joining the dead in the underworld (Sheol), not just lying in a family tomb. God had promised Abraham he would "go to your fathers in peace" and be buried "at a good old age" (15:15), and here the promise is kept word for word. Jesus cited God as "the God of Abraham" to argue that Abraham lives (Mark 12:26–27).

a: His sons Isaac and Ishmael laid him
p: The two sons who were parted (21:14) stand together at their father's burial. Each faith reads this its own way.
b: Isaac is named first, as the heir, though Ishmael is the elder. The rabbis took this as a sign that Ishmael had repented and let Isaac go before him (Bava Batra 16b; Rashi; see 21:9). Many modern readers see a quiet reconciliation, as with Jacob and Esau at Isaac's grave (35:29). In Islam, Ishmael (Isma'il) is a prophet and the elder son who helped Abraham build the Kaaba (Qur'an 2:127); the Qur'an names Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac together as fathers of the faith (2:133, 136). Jews, Christians and Muslims today sometimes point to this verse as a picture of the family of Abraham united in honoring him.

a: God blessed Isaac his son
p: The blessing promised to Abraham (12:2) now rests on Isaac, as God had said (17:19, 21).
b: The story makes a clean handover: Abraham dies, the blessing goes to Isaac, and the next story begins. Isaac settles at Beer-lahai-roi, the well where God saw Hagar (16:14) and where he met Rebekah (24:62). It is a striking choice: the heir of the promise lives at the place named by the mother of Ishmael.

a: Nebaioth
p: Several of Ishmael's sons are names of real Arabian tribes and oases known from Assyrian and Babylonian texts.
b: Kedar (Qidri) and Nebaioth (Nabayati) appear in the annals of Assyrian kings of the 700s–600s BC as Arab tribes of the Syrian desert. Dumah is the oasis of Dumat al-Jandal, and Tema is the oasis of Tayma, where the Babylonian king Nabonidus lived for ten years (about 552–543 BC). Massa is probably the people of King Lemuel (Proverbs 31:1), and Jetur the Itureans of later times. Critical scholars use these names to date the list to the first millennium BC; conservative scholars allow that tribes are often older than their first mention. Islamic genealogy, from Ibn Ishaq on, traces the Arabs of the north, and Muhammad's tribe of Quraysh, to Ishmael through Nebaioth (Nabit) or Kedar (Qaydar).

a: twelve chieftains by their clans
p: God promised Ishmael twelve princes (17:20). He gets them, as Jacob will have twelve sons.
b: The number fulfills the promise to Hagar's son (17:20) and matches the twelve tribes of Israel (35:22–26) and the twelve sons of Nahor (22:20–24). Genesis treats Ishmael's line with respect: it is a real nation, organized, settled and blessed, even though the covenant passes through Isaac. "Villages" are unwalled settlements and "camps" are circles of tents, the two ways of life of Arabian tribes.

a: He settled in the face of all his brothers
t: "He fell upon the face of his brothers"
p: The Hebrew says Ishmael "fell" before all his brothers. It recalls the oracle given to Hagar (16:12).
b: Literally "on the face of all his brothers he fell." "Fell" can mean "settled, lay encamped" (Judges 7:12), and "on the face of" can mean "in front of, east of" or "against." Hagar was told that Ishmael would live "in the face of all his brothers" (16:12), and this verse closes the circle. Older translations read hostility ("in defiance," "in hostility"); others read geography ("alongside," "to the east of"). The Plain English keeps the literal "in the face of," as at 16:12. Rashi took "fell" as "died," contrasting it with his dwelling in 16:12.

a: Bethuel the Aramean of Paddan-aram
p: Rebekah's family is called Aramean. Moses' later creed says "a wandering Aramean was my father."
b: Paddan-aram means "field of Aram" or "road of Aram," the region around Haran.
