The Arameans are firmly known from Assyrian records from about 1100 BC, so many scholars see the label as the usage of a later age for the people of that region. Conservative scholars answer that earlier names like it occur and that the term may update an older one, as "Dan" does at 14:14. Israel remembered its Aramean roots in the confession at the offering of first fruits: "My father was an Aramean close to perishing" (or "a wandering Aramean") (Deuteronomy 26:5), usually taken of Jacob.

a: for his wife
p: Isaac prays "opposite" or "on behalf of" his wife. Rebekah is the second barren matriarch.
b: The rare preposition lenokhach means "in front of, opposite." Rashi read it as a picture: Isaac stood in one corner praying and Rebekah in the other (from Genesis Rabbah 63:5). Sarah, Rebekah and Rachel are all barren at first (11:30; 29:31), so every child of the promise is a gift. The dates in 25:20 and 25:26 show a wait of twenty years. Isaac prays; Abraham had taken matters into his own hands with Hagar (16:2).

a: The children crushed against each other inside her
p: The verb is violent: the babies "crushed" each other. The Midrash made it a fight between two ways of life.
b: The verb ratsats means to crush or smash. Rebekah's words are broken: "If so, why this I?", which may mean "why am I living?" or "why is this happening to me?" The Midrash says that when she passed houses of Torah study Jacob struggled to get out, and when she passed temples of idols Esau did (Genesis Rabbah 63:6; Rashi). To "ask the LORD" usually means going to a prophet or a sanctuary; Rashi says she went to the school of Shem and Eber, whom Jewish chronology places as still alive.

a: the elder will serve the younger
t: The elder will serve the younger
p: Paul used this oracle to argue that God's choice does not depend on works (Romans 9:10–13).
b: The oracle speaks of nations: Edom and Israel. David made Edom subject (2 Samuel 8:14), and Edom later broke free (2 Kings 8:20–22), as 27:40 foresees. Paul quotes it with Malachi 1:2–3 ("Jacob I loved, Esau I hated") to show God chose before the twins "had not yet been born, and had not done anything good or bad" (Romans 9:11). Augustinian and Reformed readers find personal election here; others, including many Arminian and Orthodox readers, stress that the oracle and Malachi speak of nations and roles in history, not eternal destinies. In rabbinic thought Edom came to stand for Rome and then Christendom. A few interpreters note that the Hebrew lacks an object marker and could in theory be read the other way.

a: red, covered all over like a cloak of hair
p: Esau's looks give names to his nation and land: red (admoni) for Edom, hair (se'ar) for Seir.
b: Admoni ("red, ruddy") sounds like Edom, and se'ar ("hair") like Seir, the hill country of Edom (32:3; 36:8). The name Esau itself is not explained; some link it to an Arabic word for "hairy" or "thick-haired." David is also called admoni (1 Samuel 16:12), so the word may mean only a ruddy complexion, but the Midrash read Esau's red color as a sign of bloodshed (Genesis Rabbah 63:8). The hair will matter when Jacob deceives his father (27:11–23).
orig: אַדְמוֹנִי כֻּלּוֹ כְּאַדֶּרֶת שֵׂעָר (admoni kullo ke'adderet se'ar)

a: his hand gripping Esau's heel
p: Jacob (ya'aqov) is named from "heel" (aqev). Hosea and Esau both read more into it (Hosea 12:3; see Genesis 27:36).
b: The story connects the name with the heel. The same root can mean "to follow behind" or "to trip up, cheat" (Jeremiah 9:4), and Esau will pun on it bitterly (27:36). Hosea recalls the scene: "In the womb he grabbed his brother's heel" (Hosea 12:3). Scholars note that names of the form Yaqub-el ("may God protect") are attested among West Semitic peoples of the second millennium BC, so the name may first have been a short prayer. Isaac's age, sixty, means he married at forty and waited twenty years.

a: a quiet man
p: The word tam usually means "blameless" or "complete." Translators soften it for Jacob, the trickster.
b: Tam is the word used of Job, "whole and upright" (Job 1:1), and its relative tamim of Noah and of what God asked of Abraham (6:9; 17:1). Here most translations render it "quiet," "plain" or "mild," contrasting the tent-dweller with the hunter. Targum Onkelos calls Jacob "a perfect man, who served in the house of study," and Jewish tradition took "dwelling in tents" as the tents of Torah (Rashi). Modern readers often see the contrast of shepherd and hunter, settled and wild, and note the irony of calling Jacob tam just before he bargains Esau out of his birthright.

a: because he had a taste for game
p: Literally "for game was in his mouth." The parents' divided love sets up chapter 27.
b: Isaac loves Esau for a reason, his food; Rebekah's love for Jacob is simply stated, and the verb for hers is a continuing form ("was loving"). Rashi read "in his mouth" as Esau's mouth: Esau trapped his father with clever talk, asking questions to seem pious. The favoritism will lead to deceit and exile (27:1–28:5).

a: Let me gulp down some of that red stuff, this red stuff
p: Esau does not even name the food. His crude words give Edom ("Red") its name.
b: The verb hal'it ("let me gulp") is used in later Hebrew of stuffing food into animals (Mishnah Shabbat 24:3), and Esau repeats "the red, this red" as if he cannot find the word for stew. His speech paints a man ruled by appetite. Edom means "red"; the reddish sandstone of the Edomite hills may also lie behind the name. Jacob's coolness ("sell me ... first, today") is just as revealing.
orig: הַלְעִיטֵנִי נָא מִן־הָאָדֹם הָאָדֹם הַזֶּה (hal'iteni na min-ha'adom ha'adom hazzeh)

a: Sell me your birthright first, today
p: The firstborn received a double share (Deuteronomy 21:17). Ancient tablets record such rights being sold.
b: The birthright (bekhorah) brought a double share of the estate and leadership of the family (Deuteronomy 21:17; 1 Chronicles 5:1–2). A tablet from Nuzi in northern Mesopotamia (about 1400s BC) is often cited, in which a man gives his inheritance share to his brother for three sheep. Speiser and others used it to set the patriarchs in the second millennium; later scholars showed such parallels also exist in later periods, so they do not prove a date. Whether a birthright could legally be sold is debated, and Jacob still feels the need to take the blessing separately (27:36).

a: So Esau despised the birthright
p: The narrator's verdict falls on Esau, not Jacob. Hebrews calls Esau "godless" for this (Hebrews 12:16).
b: Five quick verbs, "he ate, drank, got up, left, despised," sum up Esau. Hebrews warns readers not to be like Esau, "who gave up his rights as firstborn for one meal" (Hebrews 12:16–17). The rabbis said that day was the day Abraham died, and the lentils were the mourners' meal Jacob cooked for Isaac; Esau came in after committing grave sins in the field (Bava Batra 16b; Genesis Rabbah 63:11–12; Rashi). Many modern readers find Jacob's bargain hard and Esau more sympathetic than the verdict allows; the story itself leaves both brothers flawed, and later chapters show the cost.
